The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the relativistic particle model, on top of the
flat spacetime model of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and the SI unit
conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], together with
the framework's idealisations of point particles, ideal clocks and ideal light
signals:

**(i) Mass and momentum.** Every massive classical particle of the model
carries a positive constant invariant mass parameter $m>0$ and has
four-momentum $P=mU$, where $U$ is the four-velocity of its future timelike
worldline ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]],
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]],
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]); $P$ is a vector of $V$
whose SI unit is kilogram metre per second. The formula is adopted only for
$m>0$; the case $m=0$ is not defined by it and is the separate premise
[[post-sr-ideal-massless-particle-momentum]]. In particular $\eta(P,P)=-m^2c^2$
is a consequence of the four-velocity normalisation, not a separate
assumption.

**(ii) Observer measurement identification.** Relative to a future unit
observer $n$, the model identifies the measured energy of the particle with
$E_n(P)$, its measured spatial momentum with $q_n(P)$, its kinetic energy with
$T_n(P)=E_n(P)-mc^2$ and its rest energy with $mc^2$, where $E_n,q_n,T_n$ are
the quantities of [[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]]; the
units are the joule, kilogram metre per second and kilogram of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. This clause is a formulation
convention identifying mathematical quantities with the quantities the model
calls measured; it is not a measurement report and no experiment is claimed.

**(iii) Isolated collision balance.** An isolated collision is represented by
a mass-specified on-shell collision datum at an event, with finite nonempty
incoming and outgoing lists of the massive particles of (i) and/or the ideal
massless particles of [[post-sr-ideal-massless-particle-momentum]], and with
no external four-momentum transfer or omitted leg. The interaction is
idealized as confined to that event. The sum of the incoming four-momenta equals the sum of the
outgoing four-momenta, in the sense of the collision data of
[[def-sr-collision-datum-and-conservation]]: the model adopts
$Q_{\mathrm{in}}=Q_{\mathrm{out}}$ for such an isolated datum. No particular
collision is asserted to occur, and no mechanism, probability, cross section
or amplitude is supplied by this clause.

**(iv) Equation of motion for a stipulated force.** Put
$H_c^+:=\{U\in C^+:\eta(U,U)=-c^2\}$. A stipulated force law is a given
map $F:D\to V$ on a given subset $D\subseteq A\times H_c^+$,
with force components in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m/\mathrm s^2$. No regularity
away from the specified worldline is assumed. Along a given $C^2$ massive worldline
$x:I\to A$ with $(x(s),U(s))\in D$ for all $s\in I$, the model's particle
equation is $m\,dU/d\tau=F(x,U)$, with
$dU/d\tau$ the proper-time derivative of
[[def-sr-proper-time-derivative-and-four-force]], so that the stipulated $F$
is the four-force of the motion. A particular force law, and the existence,
uniqueness and domain of solutions of the resulting equation, are not adopted
here and belong to a separate model.

Empirical support for these assumptions is a nonlogical relation of the
framework, not a proof; the idealisations of point particles, ideal clocks,
ideal light signals and flat spacetime are inherited and travel to every
consumer of this premise.

Consider the phase system of [[def-rpm-relativistic-coulomb-phase-system]] with $m,c,\kappa>0$. Let a trajectory have conserved energy $W>mc^2$ and angular-momentum magnitude $J:=|x\times p|>\kappa/c$. Define

$$A:=\frac{W^2-m^2c^4}{c^2}>0,\qquad d:=\frac{W\kappa}{c^2}>0,\qquad C:=J^2-\frac{\kappa^2}{c^2}>0.$$

Then its squared radial momentum is

$$p_r^2=Q(u):=A-2du-Cu^2,\qquad u:=1/r.$$

There is a unique positive simple root

$$u_*:=\frac{\sqrt{d^2+CA}-d}{C},\qquad 0<u_*<\frac{W-mc^2}{\kappa}.$$

The trajectory through the turning data $r_*=1/u_*$, $p_r=0$, and $|x\times p|=J$ is global for all system times, has one noncollision periapsis, and is asymptotically incoming and outgoing. Its impact parameter, defined as the limiting perpendicular distance of either asymptote from the force center, is

$$b=\frac{J}{\sqrt A}>0.$$

If $\Delta$ is the positive azimuthal change from either asymptote to periapsis, then

$$\Delta=\frac{J}{\sqrt C}\arctan\left(\frac{\sqrt{CA}}{d}\right),\qquad \theta:=\pi-2\Delta\in(0,\pi),$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between the incoming and outgoing asymptotic velocity vectors. This formula is for the repulsive branch $J>\kappa/c$; it does not cover $J\le\kappa/c$.

Let a massive charged test body of mass $m>0$ and charge $q$ move in flat Minkowski spacetime in the prescribed field of a fixed point source with charge $Q$, where $qQ>0$. Use SI units, $x^0=ct$, $A_0=-\phi/c$, $A_i=0$, and

$$\phi(r)=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r},\qquad \mathbf E(r)=\frac{Q\mathbf x}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^3},\qquad \mathbf B=0,\qquad \kappa:=\frac{qQ}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}>0.$$

Under the adopted fixed-endpoint charged-particle action and its proved Lorentz-force consequence, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure as required by those suppliers. In the flat specialization also adopt the massive-particle momentum model of [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]]. Then the canonical spatial momentum equals the kinetic momentum $\mathbf p=m\gamma\mathbf v$, and the coordinate-time Hamiltonian is

$$H(\mathbf x,\mathbf p)=\sqrt{m^2c^4+c^2|\mathbf p|^2}+\frac{\kappa}{r}.$$

Thus the trajectories are those of [[def-rpm-relativistic-coulomb-phase-system]]. On a scattering branch of energy $W>mc^2$ and angular-momentum magnitude $J>\kappa/c$, define

$$A=\frac{W^2-m^2c^4}{c^2},\qquad d=\frac{W\kappa}{c^2},\qquad C=J^2-\frac{\kappa^2}{c^2}.$$

Its exact angle between incoming and outgoing momenta is

$$\theta=\pi-\frac{2J}{\sqrt C}\arctan\left(\frac{\sqrt{CA}}{d}\right)\in(0,\pi).$$

This is a model deduction, not a measured scattering law. The inequality $J>\kappa/c$ is part of the result's domain; no conclusion is made for $J\le\kappa/c$.

Let $\mu>0$, let $\kappa>0$ and $U(r)=\kappa/r$ on $(0,\infty)$ (the repulsive
Coulomb potential, of class $C^2$), let $E>0$ and $J>0$, and put
$$V(r):=\frac{\kappa}{r}+\frac{J^2}{2\mu r^2},\qquad b:=\frac{J}{\sqrt{2\mu E}}>0,\qquad \alpha:=\frac{\kappa}{Eb}>0.$$
Then:

1. $V$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$, with $V(r)\to\infty$ as $r\downarrow0$
   and $V(r)\to0$ as $r\to\infty$; hence there is exactly one $r_*>0$ with
   $V(r_*)=E$, it is simple ($V'(r_*)<0$), and $V(r)<E$ for all $r>r_*$.
2. Let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with
   constant angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$, energy $E$, with $|r(t)|\ge r_*$
   for all $t\in I$ and with $|r(t_*)|=r_*$ for some $t_*\in I$. Then $r$
   extends uniquely to all of $\mathbb R$; along the extension $\rho=|r|\ge r_*>0$
   (no collision), $\rho$ is strictly decreasing on $(-\infty,t_*]$ and
   strictly increasing on $[t_*,\infty)$, and the asymptotic velocities
   $v_\pm=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}r'(t)$ exist with $|v_+|=|v_-|=\sqrt{2E/\mu}$.
   Moreover the asymptotic perpendicular distance of each branch to its
   limiting direction exists and equals
   $$b=\frac{J}{\sqrt{2\mu E}}=\frac{J}{\mu|v_\pm|}, \qquad\text{so that}\qquad J=\mu b|v_\pm| .$$
The distance in clause 2 means the limit of $|r(t)\times v_\pm|/|v_\pm|$ as $t\to\pm\infty$, the distance to the line through the origin in the limiting velocity direction; it does not assert a free tail or a finite longitudinal intercept.

3. For the polar angle, with $u_*:=1/r_*$,
   $$\Delta:=\int_{r_*}^{\infty}\frac{J\,\mathrm dr}{r^2\sqrt{2\mu\,(E-V(r))}} =\int_0^{u_*}\frac{b\,\mathrm du}{\sqrt{1-\dfrac{\kappa}{E}u-b^2u^2}} =\frac{\pi}{2}-\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}.$$

4. Write $n_\pm=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}r(t)/|r(t)|$. Then
   $n_+=v_+/|v_+|$, $n_-=-v_-/|v_-|$, and in an oriented polar plane
   the outgoing velocity direction is the incoming direction rotated by
   $2\Delta-\pi\in(-\pi,0)$. In particular
   $$\frac{\langle v_-,v_+\rangle}{|v_-||v_+|}=\cos(\pi-2\Delta),\qquad \theta_{\mathrm s}=\pi-2\Delta=2\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}.$$
   For fixed $\mu,\kappa,E$ this gives an actual family for every $b>0$,
   with angular momentum $J(b)=\sqrt{2\mu E}\,b$: choose its unique turning
   radius and initial data $r(0)=r_*e_1$, $r'(0)=J(b)e_2/(\mu r_*)$.
   Local existence and the extension in clause 2 give a member of the family
   for every $b$, unique up to apsis time and oriented plane placement.

For every $y>0$,

$$\arctan y+\arctan(1/y)=\frac{\pi}{2},$$

where $\arctan$ takes values in $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$.

By [[lem-tangent-principal-branch-is-bijective]], tangent restricts to a
continuous strictly increasing bijection

$$\tan:(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\longrightarrow\mathbb R.$$

Its inverse is the **principal inverse tangent**

$$\arctan:\mathbb R\longrightarrow(-\pi/2,\pi/2).$$

Thus $\tan(\arctan y)=y$ for every real $y$, while
$\arctan(\tan x)=x$ precisely for $x$ in the displayed principal interval.
The inverse is continuous and strictly increasing by [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

where the projections are parallel and perpendicular to $\mathbf B$.

For any acceleration $a=D_\tau U$ within the Lorentz-force model, the $G=0$ branch is Fermi–Walker transport on the orthogonal spin subspace:
$$D_\tau s=\frac{1}{c^2}\bigl(Ug(a,s)-a g(U,s)\bigr)=\frac{U}{c^2}g(a,s).$$
In an inertial rest frame with uniform $\mathbf E=0$ and constant $\mathbf B\ne0$, $U=(c,\mathbf0)$ is stationary and the $G$ branch has the exact solution
$$\mathbf s(\tau)=\mathbf s_\parallel+\cos(\omega\Delta\tau)\mathbf s_\perp-\sin(\omega\Delta\tau)\widehat{\mathbf B}\times\mathbf s_\perp,\qquad \omega=\frac{qG}{m}|\mathbf B|,\quad \Delta\tau=\tau-\tau_0,$$
where the projections are parallel and perpendicular to $\mathbf B$.

Fix $c>0$ and a future unit observer $n$ in an affine Minkowski spacetime as in [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. Identify the positive-definite rest space $n^\perp$ with $\mathbb R^3$ and its Euclidean measure $d^3x$. Let $e:\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ and $j:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be Lebesgue-integrable, both zero almost everywhere outside $\overline B_\ell(0)$ for some $\ell>0$. Suppose $|j(x)|\le e(x)/c$ almost everywhere. Define
$$E_0:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e(x)\,d^3x>0,\qquad M:=E_0/c^2,\qquad \mathbf s_*:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}x\times j(x)\,d^3x.$$
Then $\mathbf s_*$ is absolutely integrable and
$$|\mathbf s_*|\le\ell Mc,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \ell\ge\frac{|\mathbf s_*|}{Mc}.$$
The hypotheses are the full mathematical content of this estimate; it is not a bound for a quantum point particle or for a source whose energy density or momentum density fails them.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space, with signature $(-+++)$, and fix $c>0$. Let $p$ be a future timelike vector with rest-frame components $p=(Mc,\mathbf 0)$ for $M>0$. Let $S^{ab}=-S^{ba}$ satisfy the momentum supplementary condition $S^{ab}p_b=0$, and set $s_*^k:=\tfrac12\epsilon_{kij}S^{ij}$ in an oriented orthonormal rest-space basis. For every future unit observer
$$n=\gamma(1,\mathbf v/c),\qquad \gamma=(1-|\mathbf v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2},\qquad |\mathbf v|<c,$$
define
$$\delta^a:=\frac{S^{ab}n_b}{p\cdot n},\qquad S'^{ab}:=S^{ab}-(\delta^ap^b-\delta^bp^a).$$
Then $p\cdot n\ne0$, $\delta\cdot p=\delta\cdot n=0$, and $S'^{ab}n_b=0$. If the representative point changes by $z\mapsto z+\delta$, the total angular momentum $J=z\wedge p+S$ is unchanged by this stipulated spin-shift rule. In the rest space,
$$\boldsymbol\delta=\frac{\mathbf s_*\times\mathbf v}{Mc^2},$$
If $\mathbf s_*\ne0$, the shifts of all future timelike observers fill the open disk in $\mathbf s_*^\perp$ of radius $|\mathbf s_*|/(Mc)$; the boundary is a supremum and is not attained. If $\mathbf s_*=0$, only the zero shift occurs. This is an exact affine-flat algebraic result.

It is distinct from the potential-dependent covector defined in [[lem-rpm-charge-gauge-boundary]].
- The **spin or polarization vector** is a $C^1$ tangent vector field $s(\tau)\in T_{z(\tau)}M$ constrained by $g(s,U)=0$, so it lies in the positive-definite instantaneous rest space $U^\perp$.

Substitution in that theorem gives the displayed $\mathbf s(\tau)$; differentiating yields $d\mathbf s/d\tau=\omega s_0[-\sin(\omega\Delta\tau)\mathbf e_1-\cos(\omega\Delta\tau)\mathbf e_2]$, equal to $\alpha G(\mathbf s\times B\mathbf e_3)$. The initial value at $\tau_0$ is $s_0\mathbf e_1$.

Use the flat affine Minkowski model with signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and SI coordinates $(x^0,x^1,y,z)=(ct,x^1,y,z)$. Fix $a>0$ in metres per second squared and define

$$\Phi_a(T,\rho,y,z)=\bigl(\rho\sinh(aT/c),\rho\cosh(aT/c),y,z\bigr),\qquad T\in\mathbb R,\quad \rho>0.$$

Then $\Phi_a$ is a smooth chart of the right wedge $W=\{x^1>|x^0|\}$, with $\rho$ in metres and $T$ in seconds. Its pullback metric, the proper-time rate of a stationary Rindler observer, and that observer's proper-acceleration magnitude are

$$ds^2=-\frac{a^2\rho^2}{c^2}\,dT^2+d\rho^2+dy^2+dz^2,\qquad \frac{d\tau}{dT}=\frac{a\rho}{c^2},\qquad \alpha=\frac{c^2}{\rho}.$$

For ideal radial vacuum rays with $y,z$ fixed, $d\rho/dT=\pm a\rho/c$. A ray joining positive radii $\rho_E,\rho_R$ therefore has one-way Rindler travel time $\Delta T=(c/a)|\log(\rho_R/\rho_E)|$, and stationary ideal clocks at those radii satisfy $\Delta\tau_R/\Delta\tau_E=\rho_R/\rho_E$ over any common nonzero $T$ interval. The clock statement is conditional on the ideal-clock adoption in [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]].

For a future null plane-wave covector $k$ directed along the same radial ray, define $\omega_n=-k(U_n)$ using [[def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency]]. Under the additional adopted local reception rule [[post-rpm-ideal-rindler-phase-reception]], the instantaneous received angular frequencies at the two events obey $\omega_R/\omega_E=\rho_E/\rho_R$. The ratio is exact within that ideal model and inherits its local ray-regime and finite-apparatus qualifications, with no numerical error bound or empirical validation. Clause (iv) of [[post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model]] retains its accelerated-reception exclusion; this theorem uses the separately adopted rule. The coordinate chart excludes $\rho=0$; no global rigid accelerated frame is asserted.

The clock-gradient formula gives $\Delta\tau_R/\Delta\tau_E=\rho_R/\rho_E=4\,\mathrm m/(2\,\mathrm m)=2$. The contraction functional gives $\omega_R/\omega_E=\rho_E/\rho_R=1/2$. Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum with $s>0$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$ on $r>s$. Let $\gamma(\lambda)$ be an affinely parametrized null geodesic of its metric-selected connection whose image lies in the equatorial plane $\vartheta=\pi/2$, and choose the orientation so that

$$E:=f(r)\frac{dx^0}{d\lambda}>0,\qquad L:=r^2\frac{d\varphi}{d\lambda}\ge0.$$

Both quantities are constant along $\gamma$. With impact parameter $b:=L/E\ge0$ and $H(r):=f(r)/r^2$, its radial equation is

$$\left(\frac{dr}{d\lambda}\right)^2=E^2\bigl(1-b^2H(r)\bigr).$$

Moreover, $H'(r)=(3s-2r)/r^4$, so $H$ has its unique exterior maximum at $r_{\rm ph}=3s/2$, with $H(r_{\rm ph})=4/(27s^2)$. Thus the critical impact parameter for a radial turning point is $b_{\rm c}=3\sqrt3\,s/2$.

Adopt the Schwarzschild exterior vacuum model with $s>0$ and the ideal-light rule that rays are future null geodesics. For an equatorial incoming ray with constants $E>0$, $L\ge0$, impact parameter $b=L/E$, and

$$H(r)=\frac{1-s/r}{r^2},\qquad b_{\rm c}=\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}s,\qquad r_{\rm ph}=\frac32s,$$

the radial first integral is $\dot r^2=E^2[1-b^2H(r)]$ as in [[lem-rpm-schwarzschild-null-geodesic-reduction]], where dot denotes affine-parameter derivative. Then:

1. If $b>b_{\rm c}$, there is a unique outer turning point $r_*(b)>r_{\rm ph}$, which is reached in finite affine parameter; the ray from infinity turns and returns to infinity. Its total azimuthal advance is

   $$\Delta\varphi=2\int_{r_*}^{\infty}\frac{b\,dr}{r^2\sqrt{1-b^2H(r)}}.$$

   This integral converges at both endpoints.
2. If $b=b_{\rm c}$, the incoming branch from infinity approaches $r_{\rm ph}$ only as affine parameter tends to $+\infty$; its azimuthal advance diverges logarithmically.
3. If $0\le b<b_{\rm c}$, the inward branch has no exterior turning point and reaches the boundary $r=s$ of the Schwarzschild exterior in finite affine parameter. Only if the ray is continued in the specified Kruskal model, once it lies in the region $U\ge0$, does the causal escape result imply that it cannot return to the right exterior.

These are geodesic-model deductions. The impact threshold is not by itself an observable shadow radius.

derivations.claim: Since $(2\sqrt2s)^2=8s^2$ and $H(2s)=1/(8s^2)$, the radial factor vanishes at $2s$. Also $2\sqrt2s>3\sqrt3s/2$ because $32>27$, and $H$ is strictly decreasing above $3s/2$, so this is the unique outer root. The turning and return classification follows from [F2].

Substituting $b_c^2=27s^2/4$ and $H=(r-s)/r^3$ and expanding the numerator verifies the displayed factorization. The double zero at $r=3s/2$ and the theorem's affine and angular quadratures then give the critical asymptote and logarithmic divergence.
These are exact ideal-geodesic conclusions in the Schwarzschild model; no wave-optics or observational statement is added.

citations.quote:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum with $s>0$ and
$f(r)=1-s/r$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), with
$f'=s/r^2$. Then:

For arbitrary $x^0_0,\varphi_0\in\mathbb R$, put
$\omega_0=(\cos\varphi_0,\sin\varphi_0,0)\in S^2$. For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$
define the rotation
$$R_\alpha(y_1,y_2,y_3):=(y_1\cos\alpha-y_2\sin\alpha,\ y_1\sin\alpha+y_2\cos\alpha,\ y_3),$$
and the global axial vector field $\Phi(y_1,y_2,y_3):=(-y_2,y_1,0)$ on $S^2$;
it is tangent because $y\cdot\Phi(y)=0$ for $y\in S^2$.
In every spherical-polar chart near the equator, $\Phi=\partial_\varphi$;
longitude expressions below are local chart expressions for the global sphere
curve $R_\alpha\omega_0$.

In this item, a **timelike circular geodesic** means a future timelike
geodesic whose areal radius $r$ is constant on an interval of positive length;
its angular orientation is unrestricted.

**(a) Existence of circular timelike geodesics.** Let $r_0>3s/2$ and choose
$\ell\in\mathbb R$ with

$$\ell^2=\frac{c^2sr_0^2}{2r_0-3s}>0,\qquad e:=\Bigl(f(r_0)\Bigl(c^2+\frac{\ell^2}{r_0^2}\Bigr)\Bigr)^{1/2} =\frac{c(r_0-s)\sqrt 2}{\sqrt{r_0(2r_0-3s)}}>0 .$$

Then the globally defined curve $\gamma:\mathbb R\to M$ is

$$\gamma(\tau):=\bigl(x^0_0+\tfrac{e}{f(r_0)}\tau,\ r_0,\ R_{\ell\tau/r_0^2}\omega_0\bigr).$$
In each local polar chart along it, $\vartheta=\pi/2$ and the longitude is
$\varphi_0+\ell\tau/r_0^2$ up to a constant multiple of $2\pi$.

It is a future timelike geodesic of the datum, with $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-c^2$
and with the conserved quantities $e=-g(\gamma',\partial_0)$ and
$\ell=g(\gamma',\Phi)$ of
[[lem-gr-schwarzschild-timelike-geodesic-reduction]]; it is a **circular
orbit** at radius $r_0$. Its angular velocity in the coordinate $x^0$ is

$$\frac{d\varphi}{dx^0}=\frac{\ell f(r_0)}{r_0^2e}=\operatorname{sgn}(\ell)\Bigl(\frac{s}{2r_0^3}\Bigr)^{1/2},\qquad\text{so}\qquad \Bigl(\frac{d\varphi}{dt}\Bigr)^2=\frac{G_Nm_*}{r_0^3},$$

$t=x^0/c$.

**(b) The circular-orbit condition is necessary.** Conversely, if
$\gamma:I\to M$ is any future timelike geodesic parametrized by proper time with
$r(\tau)\equiv r_0>s$ constant on an interval of positive length, then
$r_0>\frac{3s}{2}$. If $\gamma$ is equatorial, its conserved angular
momentum additionally satisfies $\ell^2=\dfrac{c^2sr_0^2}{2r_0-3s}$.
Consequently no timelike circular geodesic, in any angular orientation, exists
with $s<r_0\le\frac{3s}{2}$.

**(c) Stability threshold of the radial potential.** For each radius
$r>\frac{3s}{2}$ set $\ell_r^2:=c^2sr^2/(2r-3s)$ and regard $\ell_r$ as a
constant in the function $V_{\ell_r}(x):=\tfrac12 f(x)(c^2+\ell_r^2/x^2)$.
Differentiate with respect to $x$ at fixed $\ell_r$, then evaluate at $x=r$.
The result, evaluated at the circular value $\ell_r$, is

$$V_{\ell_r}''(r)=\frac{c^2s(r-3s)}{r^3(2r-3s)},\qquad r>\frac{3s}{2},$$

so $V_\ell$ has a strict local minimum at the circular-orbit radius exactly
for $r>3s$, a strict local maximum exactly for $\frac{3s}{2}<r<3s$, and
$V_\ell''(3s)=0$; the radius $r=3s$ is the **innermost stable circular orbit
radius** of the restricted model in this potential sense.

**(d) The photon sphere at $r=3s/2$.** Let $\ell\neq0$ and put
$r_0=\frac{3s}{2}$ and $e_0:=\dfrac{\lvert\ell\rvert\sqrt{f(r_0)}}{r_0}=\dfrac{2\lvert\ell\rvert}{3\sqrt3\,s}>0$.
Then the globally defined curve
$$\eta(\tau):=\bigl(x^0_0+\tfrac{e_0}{f(r_0)}\tau,\ r_0,\ R_{\ell\tau/r_0^2}\omega_0\bigr),\qquad \tau\in\mathbb R,$$
whose local polar expressions have $\vartheta=\pi/2$ and longitude
$\varphi_0+\ell\tau/r_0^2$ up to chart shifts, is a future null geodesic (a
**null circular orbit** or **photon sphere**
orbit) with conserved quantities $e_0=-g(\eta',\partial_0)$ and
$\ell=g(\eta',\Phi)$, and its angular velocity is

$$\frac{d\varphi}{dx^0}=\frac{\ell f(r_0)}{r_0^2e_0}=\operatorname{sgn}(\ell)\,\frac{\sqrt{f(r_0)}}{r_0},\qquad \Bigl(\frac{d\varphi}{dx^0}\Bigr)^2=\frac{f(r_0)}{r_0^2}=\frac{4}{27s^2}.$$

The **null effective potential** $W^{\mathrm n}_\ell(r):=f(r)\ell^2/r^2$
satisfies $(W^{\mathrm n}_\ell)'(3s/2)=0$ and
$(W^{\mathrm n}_\ell)''(3s/2)=-\dfrac{32\ell^2}{81s^4}<0$, so the photon-sphere
radius is a strict local maximum of the null potential.

**(e) Scope.** All statements are exact data of the restricted model: the
orbits are ideal geodesics of the metric on the exterior domain, the
stability claim is the sign of the second derivative of the stated potential,
and no claim is made about nonlinear stability, about orbital decay, about
observations or about the interior region. The case $r_0=s$ is excluded, and
the reduction is stated only where $r>s$.

Adopt the Schwarzschild vacuum exterior model with $m_*>0$, $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2>0$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$, together with its ideal-free-fall rule that a massive test body follows a future timelike geodesic. For a fixed angular-momentum magnitude $\ell>0$, set

$$W_\ell(r)=f(r)\left(c^2+\frac{\ell^2}{r^2}\right),\qquad r>s.$$

The equatorial reduced radial system is

$$\dot r=w,\qquad \dot w=-\frac12 W_\ell'(r),$$

where dot denotes proper-time derivative and $\ell$ is held fixed. For every circular timelike radius $r_c>3s/2$, the corresponding equilibrium is

$$z_c=(r_c,0),\qquad \ell^2=\frac{c^2s r_c^2}{2r_c-3s}.$$

Then this equilibrium is Lyapunov stable in the Euclidean phase space $(r,w)$ when $r_c>3s$, and is not Lyapunov stable when $3s/2<r_c\le3s$. At $r_c=3s$ the equilibrium is a stationary inflection of $W_\ell$, not a strict extremum, and is still not Lyapunov stable. These are conclusions about the reduced radial system at fixed $\ell$ only.

derivations.claim: At $r_0=4s$, substitution gives $\ell^2=c^2s(16s^2)/(8s-3s)=16c^2s^2/5$ and [F1] gives $W_\ell''=2V_\ell''=c^2/(160s^2)>0$. Since $4s>3s$, [F2] classifies the equilibrium as Lyapunov stable in the fixed-$\ell$ radial state.
At $r_0=2s$, substitution gives $\ell^2=4c^2s^2$ and $W_\ell''=2V_\ell''=-c^2/(4s^2)<0$. Since $3s/2<2s<3s$, [F2] classifies this equilibrium as unstable.

At $r_0=3s$, substitution gives $\ell^2=3c^2s^2$. The formula for $W_\ell'$ in [F1] at this angular momentum is $c^2s(r-3s)^2/r^4$, positive away from $3s$ and zero at $3s$. The equilibrium is a stationary inflection; [F2] classifies it as not Lyapunov stable. All three results are restricted radial-model classifications.

Let $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2>0$, $f(r)=1-s/r$, and let $r_E,r_R>s$ be the emitter and receiver radii of static observers in the adopted Schwarzschild exterior model. With $n=f^{-1/2}\partial_0$ the unit static congruence and $U=cn$ the corresponding four-velocity, the ideal-clock and geometric-optics predictions are

$$\frac{\Delta\tau_R}{\Delta\tau_E}=\frac{\omega_E}{\omega_R}=\sqrt{\frac{f(r_R)}{f(r_E)}},\qquad \frac{\omega_R}{\omega_E}=\sqrt{\frac{f(r_E)}{f(r_R)}}.$$

The proper four-acceleration magnitude required to remain static at radius $r>s$ is

$$a(r)=\sqrt{g(\nabla_UU,\nabla_UU)}=\frac{c^2s}{2r^2\sqrt{f(r)}}=\frac{G_Nm_*}{r^2\sqrt{1-s/r}}.$$

For any $0\le\rho<1$ and radii satisfying $0<s/r_E,s/r_R\le\rho$, define $x_i=s/r_i$ and write $\log:=L$ for the natural integral logarithm of [[def-integral-logarithm]]. The exact logarithmic ratio has the uniform expansion

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum of mass parameter $m_*$,
Schwarzschild radius $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), with curvature data as in
[[lem-gr-schwarzschild-ricci-and-einstein-tensors]]. On each spherical-polar
product chart $(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ define the local frame field

$$e_{\hat0}:=f^{-1/2}\partial_0,\qquad e_{\hat1}:=f^{1/2}\partial_1,\qquad e_{\hat2}:=r^{-1}\partial_2,\qquad e_{\hat3}:=(r\sin\vartheta)^{-1}\partial_3,$$

and for the curvature tensor define the **frame components**

$$\hat R_{\hat a\hat b\hat c\hat d}:=g\bigl(R(e_{\hat c},e_{\hat d})e_{\hat b},e_{\hat a}\bigr).$$

Then:

**(a) The frame field.** $(e_{\hat0},e_{\hat1},e_{\hat2},e_{\hat3})$ is a
smooth $g$-orthonormal frame (tetrad field) on the chart domain, with
$g(e_{\hat a},e_{\hat b})=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{\hat a\hat b}$, and
$e_{\hat0}$ is future-directed timelike; it is a tetrad field in the sense of
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. It is not a coordinate frame.

**(b) Frame components.** The nonzero frame components, up to the
symmetries $R_{abcd}=-R_{bacd}=-R_{abdc}=R_{cdab}$ of
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]], are

$$\hat R_{\hat0\hat1\hat0\hat1}=\frac{f''}{2},\qquad \hat R_{\hat0\hat2\hat0\hat2}=\hat R_{\hat0\hat3\hat0\hat3}=\frac{f'}{2r},$$

$$\hat R_{\hat1\hat2\hat1\hat2}=\hat R_{\hat1\hat3\hat1\hat3}=-\frac{f'}{2r},\qquad \hat R_{\hat2\hat3\hat2\hat3}=\frac{1-f}{r^2},$$

with $f'=s/r^2$ and $f''=-2s/r^3$; all other frame components vanish.

**(c) Kretschmann scalar.** Define the global smooth scalar field
$K:=R_{abcd}R^{abcd}$, with indices raised by the inverse metric. On the
spherical-polar chart locus its component expression is

$$K=f''^2+\frac{4(f')^2}{r^2}+\frac{4(1-f)^2}{r^4},$$

and for the model function $f=1-s/r$ this is

$$K=\frac{12s^2}{r^6}=\frac{48\,G_N^2m_*^2}{c^4\,r^6}.$$

The scalar identity is first computed on the regular angular locus and holds
on all of $M$ by smoothness and density. Since $r>s$ on $M$, one has
$0<K=12s^2/r^6<12/s^4$ at every point; as $r\downarrow s$ the expression has
the finite boundary value $12/s^4$, and the expression $12s^2/r^6$, read as a
function of $r>0$, grows without bound as $r\downarrow0$.

**(d) Scope.** The lemma computes curvature data of the exterior datum on
$r>s$. The limit $r\downarrow s$ is the boundary value on $M$ of the smooth
expression $12s^2/r^6$; no value of the metric at $r=s$ or at $r=0$ is used
or asserted here, those regions being outside the datum (the regular
continuation across $r=s$ is the separate extension lemma of this page).

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum with Schwarzschild radius
$s>0$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]). Let
$M_{\mathrm{ext}}:=\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)\times S^2$ carry the product
smooth structure and let $\iota_{\mathrm{ext}}:M_{\mathrm{ext}}\to S^2$ be the
third projection. Its product atlas includes ordinary sphere charts at the
poles ([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]]).
Define the **tortoise function**

$$r_*(r):=r+s\log\left|\frac{r}{s}-1\right|,\qquad r>0,\ r\ne s,$$

on each of the two intervals $(0,s)$ and $(s,\infty)$, and define the
**advanced-chart metric** globally on $M_{\mathrm{ext}}$ by

$$g_{\mathrm{ext}}=-f(r)\,dv\otimes dv+dv\otimes dr+dr\otimes dv+r^2\,\iota_{\mathrm{ext}}^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In spherical-polar product charts its components are

$$g_{\mathrm{ext}}=-f(r)\,dv^2+2\,dv\,dr+r^2\,d\Omega^2,$$

namely $g_{vv}=-f$, $g_{vr}=g_{rv}=1$,
$g_{\vartheta\vartheta}=r^2$, $g_{\varphi\varphi}=r^2\sin^2\vartheta$ and all
other components zero. In another sphere chart the angular block is
$r^2(\gamma_{ij})$. Then:

**(a) Smooth Lorentzian metric.** $g_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field on $M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and at every point it is
nondegenerate with inertia $(3,1,0)$; hence $(M_{\mathrm{ext}},g_{\mathrm{ext}})$
is a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on all of
$r>0$, including $r=s$.

**(b) Time orientation.** The smooth vector field

$$N_{\mathrm{ext}}:=A(r)\,\partial_v-\partial_r,\qquad A(r):=\frac{f(r)+\sqrt{f(r)^2+4}}{2}>0,$$

satisfies $g_{\mathrm{ext}}(N_{\mathrm{ext}},N_{\mathrm{ext}})<0$ everywhere
and $g_{\mathrm{ext}}(N_{\mathrm{ext}},\partial_v)<0$ everywhere; hence
$N_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is a time orientation of $g_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and on the
region $r>s$ it determines the same future cone as the datum's time
orientation $\partial_v=\partial_0$.

**(c) Isometric embedding of the exterior.** The map
$\Phi:M\to M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, $(x^0,r,\omega)\mapsto(x^0+r_*(r),r,\omega)$
restricts to a diffeomorphism of $M$ onto the open subset $\{r>s\}$ of
$M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and $\Phi^*g_{\mathrm{ext}}=g$; the exterior datum is
therefore isometric to the region $r>s$ of the extension.

**(d) Vacuum and Kretschmann scalar of the extension.** The
metric-selected connection of $g_{\mathrm{ext}}$ exists and is unique, its
Ricci tensor, scalar curvature and Einstein tensor vanish identically on
$M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and its Kretschmann scalar equals

$$R_{abcd}R^{abcd}=\frac{12s^2}{r^6}$$

on all of $M_{\mathrm{ext}}$. In particular the scalar is smooth and finite on
the horizon $r=s$, where it takes the value $12/s^4$.

**(e) The horizon is a null hypersurface.** The level set $\{r=s\}$ is a
smooth null hypersurface of $(M_{\mathrm{ext}},g_{\mathrm{ext}})$ whose null
generator direction is $\partial_v$; every smooth product-chart frame remains
a basis across $r=s$. In spherical-polar charts
$\det(g_{\mathrm{ext}})=-r^4\sin^2\vartheta$; in an arbitrary sphere chart
the determinant is $-r^4\det(\gamma_{ij})$, which is nonzero.

**(f) Scope.** The extension constructed here is a smooth Lorentzian
manifold containing the exterior isometrically and regular across $r=s$; it
is not claimed to be maximal, and no uniqueness or global structure theorem
is asserted. The region $r\le0$ and the surfaces relevant to the Kruskal
model of this page are outside this statement.

**(c) Tetrad fields.** A **tetrad field** (or **$g$-orthonormal frame field**) on $U$ is a local frame field $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ on $U$ such that $$g_q(E_A(q),E_B(q))=\eta_{AB}\qquad\text{for all }A,B\text{ and all }q\in U .$$ A tetrad field is **future-directed** when in addition $E_0(q)$ is future-directed for every $q\in U$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]); then each $E_0(q)$ is an observer at $q$ ([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]), so $E_0$ is an observer congruence on $U$ ([[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]), while $E_1,E_2,E_3$ are pointwise an orthonormal basis of the rest space of that observer.

That these local forms agree on chart overlaps and therefore define one smooth nowhere-vanishing $4$-form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ on $M$ — the **metric volume form** — is proved in [[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (a), together with the reading statement of clause (b) there: in every oriented chart $\mathrm{vol}_g=w\,dx^0\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^3$, and on every positively oriented $g_p$-orthonormal basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $T_pM$ one has $\mathrm{vol}_{g,p}(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=1$.

Then $$\det(g'_{ab})=\bigl(\det D\varphi\bigr)^{2}\det\bigl(g_{ab}\circ\varphi\bigr),\qquad w'=\bigl(\det D\varphi\bigr)\,(w\circ\varphi),$$ and the local forms agree on the overlap, $$\varphi^{*}\bigl(w\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3\bigr)=w'\,dy^0\wedge dy^1\wedge dy^2\wedge dy^3 .$$ Consequently there is a unique smooth nowhere-vanishing $4$-form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ on $M$ — the **metric volume form** — whose restriction to the domain of every oriented chart $(U,x)$ is $w\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$; it is a smooth section with nowhere-zero values and positive on the given orientation.
A **smooth differential $k$-form** on $M$ is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M\to M$.

On a chart $(U,x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, every smooth differential $k$-form $\omega$ has a unique expression $$ \omega=\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n}\omega_{i_1\cdots i_k}\,dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k} $$ with smooth coefficient functions $\omega_{i_1\cdots i_k}$ on $U$.
Their **wedge product** is the differential form defined pointwise by $$ (\alpha\wedge\beta)_p:=\alpha_p\wedge\beta_p\in\operatorname{Alt}^{k+\ell}(T_pM).
The graded vector space $$ \Omega^*(M):=\bigoplus_{k\ge 0}\Omega^k(M) $$ with the wedge product is an associative graded-commutative algebra.

For $\omega\in\Omega^k(M)$, define the candidate $d\omega$ on smooth vector fields by $$d\omega(X_0,\ldots,X_k)=\sum_i(-1)^iX_i\omega(X_0,\widehat X_i,\ldots,X_k)+\sum_{i<j}(-1)^{i+j}\omega([X_i,X_j],X_0,\widehat X_i,\widehat X_j,\ldots,X_k).$$ The next lemma proves that this candidate is a form.
The invariant formula defining $d\omega$ is alternating and $C^\infty(M)$-multilinear in $X_0,\ldots,X_k$; hence it defines a smooth $(k+1)$-form.
Summing over increasing $k$-tuples $I$, and writing $dx^I=dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$, if $\omega=\sum_I\omega_I\,dx^I$, then $$d\omega=\sum_I d\omega_I\wedge dx^I.$$
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.
For homogeneous smooth forms $\alpha\in\Omega^p(M)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^q(M)$, $$d(\alpha\wedge\beta)=d\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^{\deg\alpha}\alpha\wedge d\beta.$$

**Inverse metric.** The **inverse metric** at $p$ is the symmetric bilinear form $$g_p^{-1}:T_p^*M\times T_p^*M\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta).$$ It is symmetric because $g_p$ is, and it is nondegenerate: if $g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)=0$ for all $\beta$, then $g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\cdot)=0$, so $\sharp_p\alpha=0$ and hence $\alpha=0$.
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following statement.

derivations.claim: The determinant is alternating multilinear in each list, so it defines a bilinear pairing on exterior powers. In a positively oriented orthonormal coframe, it makes the basis wedges $e^I$ orthogonal with squared norm $\epsilon_I$; in the full component contraction this same diagonal value occurs $k!$ times, canceled by the factor $1/k!$. Define $\star_g e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}$ and extend linearly. If $J\ne I$ has the same size as $I$, then $e^J\wedge e^{I^c}=0$ because an index repeats. If $J=I$, then $e^I\wedge e^{I^c}=s(I,I^c)\mathrm{vol}_g$, so $e^I\wedge\star_g e^I=\epsilon_I\mathrm{vol}_g$. Bilinearity proves the characterizing identity for all forms in the coframe. The complement wedges pair each basis vector with exactly one basis vector, so this wedge pairing is nondegenerate and the characterization determines $\star_g$ uniquely.

The characterizing identity uses only $g$, the orientation, and $\mathrm{vol}_g$. Any other positively oriented orthonormal coframe therefore defines the same map by uniqueness. In each smooth tetrad neighborhood the displayed matrix of $\star_g$ is constant in the smooth coframe, so its coordinate coefficients are smooth; the locally defined maps agree on overlaps and give a global smooth bundle map on the inherited smooth background [A1].

Applying the basis formula twice gives $\star_g^2e^I=\epsilon_I\epsilon_{I^c}s(I,I^c)s(I^c,I)e^I$. The product $\epsilon_I\epsilon_{I^c}$ equals $-1$ because exactly one of the four $\epsilon_i$ is negative. derivations.claim: Write $T_\epsilon=\partial_sH$ and $J=\partial_\epsilon H|_0$. Differentiating $\ell_\epsilon=\sqrt{-g(T_\epsilon,T_\epsilon)}$ and using metric compatibility gives $\partial_\epsilon\ell|_0=-g(D_\epsilon T,T)/\ell$. In a chart, the difference of the two covariant derivatives is $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(J^bT^c-T^bJ^c)$; it vanishes because [F9] gives $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\Gamma^a{}_{cb}$ and coordinate mixed partials commute by [F6]. Thus $D_\epsilon T=D_sJ$. By [F6], mixed derivatives commute; [F2] permits differentiation through the compact integral, so $\delta S=mc\int_a^b g(D_sJ,T/\ell)\,ds$.

Metric compatibility gives $\frac{d}{ds}g(J,T/\ell)=g(D_sJ,T/\ell)+g(J,D_s(T/\ell))$. Integrating and applying [F3], the boundary term vanishes because $J(a)=J(b)=0$, yielding the displayed first-variation formula.

If $D_s(T/\ell)=0$, step 2.1 makes every fixed-endpoint first variation vanish. Conversely, if this continuous vector field is nonzero at an interior point, [F5] gives a local chart component field $Z$ with $g(Z,D_s(T/\ell))$ strictly positive on a smaller interval. Multiply $Z$ by the nonnegative bump [F4], equal to $1$ near that point. Choose the support inside one chart interval and define $H(\epsilon,s)=\chi^{-1}(\chi(x(s))+\epsilon J^{\mathrm{coord}}(s))$ there for a chart $\chi$, with $H=x$ off the support. The compact support makes this a $C^2$ fixed-endpoint variation; timelikeness persists for small $|\epsilon|$ by openness and compactness. The pairing is bounded below by some $\delta>0$ on an interval where the bump equals $1$, so [F8] makes the integral in step 2.1 strictly positive and its prefactor $-mc<0$ makes the variation nonzero, a contradiction. Thus stationarity forces $D_s(T/\ell)=0$ everywhere; a nonzero endpoint value would by continuity give a nonzero interior value.

Since $U=cT/\ell$ and $d\tau/ds=\ell/c$, the chain rule gives $D_s(T/\ell)=(\ell/c^2)D_\tau U$, so the two equations are equivalent. If $s=\phi(r)$ with $\phi'>0$, then $T_r=\phi'T$ and $\ell_r=\phi'\ell$, and [F7] leaves $\int\ell ds$ unchanged; hence the action is reparametrization invariant.

citations.quote:
An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with the following data. In this notation $V$ includes its
specified orientation; forgetting that orientation gives only the underlying
real vector space, not the full datum $V$ of the model.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are
  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when
  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**No point of $A$ is distinguished.** For every $v\in V$ the translation
$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to
$\tau_{-v}$: $\tau_{-v}(\tau_v(p))=(p+v)+(-v)=p+(v-v)=p$ and symmetrically, by
the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves
the interval, the causal classification of every ordered pair, and the sets
$C^+$, $C^-$ (which are subsets of $V$, independent of the point of $A$); it
changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is
exactly the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; no derived physical quantity (proper
time, four-velocity, momentum, energy, charge or any field) is part of this
definition, and all later structure of the framework (frames, charts, tensor
fields, worldlines) is built on this model.

**Well-definedness.** The affine-space definition supplies the action and the
unique displacements; the Lorentz-form definition supplies $\eta$ and its
inertia; the determinant-line definition supplies orientations; and the two
components of $T$ between which the time-orientation definition chooses exist by
the components lemma recorded in the well-definedness clause of
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], which is also what makes the
names future and past causal in item 4 well defined.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

derivations.claim: Antisymmetry gives $\eta(U,f_0)=\alpha U^aF_{ab}U^b=0$. On the unit shell, $U_a\Pi_U{}^a{}_b=U_b+(\eta(U,U)/c^2)U_b=0$, so $\eta(U,a_{\rm LL})=0$. The coordinate right-hand side $(U,a_{\rm LL}(x,U))$ is $C^1$ on the open state domain $O\times V$: $F$ is $C^2$, its partials [F3] are $C^1$, and the remaining factors are polynomial in $U$, using [F4]. In a closed coordinate box around any state, its continuous first derivatives are bounded by [F6]; applying [F7] componentwise along line segments proves the field locally Lipschitz. Thus [F5] gives a unique local full-state solution through $(x_0,U_0)$.

For arbitrary $U$, antisymmetry gives $\eta(U,f_0)=0$ and the projector formula gives $\eta(U,\Pi_U B)=(1+\eta(U,U)/c^2)\eta(U,B)$. Along the full solution put $h(\tau)=\eta(U,U)+c^2$; then
$$h'(\tau)=2\eta(U,a_{\rm LL})=\frac{2\tau_e}{c^2}\eta(U,B)h(\tau).$$
The coefficient is continuous. The zero function solves this scalar linear IVP with $h(0)=0$, and the scalar vector field is locally Lipschitz in $h$ because it is linear in that variable, so uniqueness [F5] gives $h=0$ on the full common interval. Thus the proper-time normalization $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ is preserved.

In the inertial frame of [F2], $e_0$ has coordinates $(1,0,0,0)$. For any future timelike $W$, convexity of $C^+$ makes $(1-s)e_0+sW$ timelike for $0\le s\le1$. A timelike vector cannot have zeroth component zero, since then its squared norm would be the nonnegative spatial norm square. If $W^0\le0$, the continuous zeroth component along this segment takes the value zero by [F8], a contradiction. Thus every future timelike vector has $W^0>0$. Along the solution, the preserved shell makes $U$ timelike; if $U^0$ became nonpositive, [F8] on the closed interval between that time and $0$ would force a zero component, again impossible. Since the initial vector is future, $U$ remains in $C^+$ throughout the local interval. No continuation beyond this interval is asserted.

Step 1.2 constructs a solution on an open interval about the initial proper-time value; no endpoint extension is claimed.

Let $m,c>0$, let $0<\delta<1$, and let $v\in\mathbb R^3$ have Euclidean norm satisfying $|v|/c\le\delta$. Put

$$z:=\frac{|v|^2}{c^2},\qquad \gamma:=(1-z)^{-1/2},\qquad p:=m\gamma v,\qquad E:=\gamma mc^2.$$

Then

$$0\le\gamma-1\le\frac{z}{2(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}},\qquad 0\le\gamma-1-\frac z2\le\frac{3z^2}{8(1-\delta^2)^{5/2}},$$

and

$$|p-mv|\le\frac{m|v|^3}{2c^2(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}},\qquad 0\le E-mc^2-\frac12m|v|^2\le\frac{3m|v|^4}{8c^2(1-\delta^2)^{5/2}}.$$

If assigned SI kinematic units, $m$ is in kilograms, $c,v$ in metres per second, $p$ in kilogram metres per second and $E$ in joules. These are pointwise algebraic inequalities; they assume no equation of motion or empirical input.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as functions on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$\bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)\,g'(c) \;=\; \bigl(g(b)-g(a)\bigr)\,f'(c) .$$

**The statement is a product identity, and that is deliberate.** The familiar
quotient form

$$\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{g(b)-g(a)} \;=\; \frac{f'(c)}{g'(c)}$$

is not asserted here, and it is not equivalent: its left side needs
$g(b) \ne g(a)$ and its right side needs $g'(c) \ne 0$, and neither follows from
the hypotheses. The product form above needs neither, holds under exactly the
hypotheses stated, and specialises to the quotient form whenever both
denominators happen to be nonzero. The companion page exhibits an $f$ and a $g$
for which the quotient form is meaningless while the product form holds.

derivations.claim: From $|v|\le C\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,c$ and $\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_*$, $z=|v|^2/c^2\le C^2\varepsilon\le\rho$. Apply [L1] with $\delta=\sqrt\rho$ and then use $z\le C^2\varepsilon$: the gamma remainder is at most $3C^4\varepsilon^2/[8(1-\rho)^{5/2}]$, the momentum error is at most $mC^3c\varepsilon^{3/2}/[2(1-\rho)^{3/2}]$, and the energy remainder is at most $3mC^4c^2\varepsilon^2/[8(1-\rho)^{5/2}]$. The first-order gamma bound follows from $z\le C^2\varepsilon$ in the same way.

Put $f(s)=\sqrt{1-s}=(1-s)^{1/2}$ on $[0,\rho]$. By [L2], $f(0)=1$, $f'(0)=-1/2$, and $|f''(s)|=\frac14(1-s)^{-3/2}$; differentiating $(1-s)^{-3/2}$ gives the positive derivative $\frac32(1-s)^{-5/2}$, so this absolute value is increasing and bounded above by $\frac14(1-\rho)^{-3/2}$. For $z>0$, set $q(s)=f(s)-1+s/2$ and $g(s)=s^2$ on $[0,z]$. Since $q(0)=g(0)=0$, [L3] supplies $\xi\in(0,z)$ with $q(z)=z^2q'(\xi)/(2\xi)$. The mean value theorem applied to $f'$ on $[0,\xi]$ gives $\eta\in(0,\xi)$ such that $q'(\xi)=f'(\xi)-f'(0)=\xi f''(\eta)$. Hence $|q(z)|=\frac12z^2|f''(\eta)|\le z^2/[8(1-\rho)^{3/2}]$. The same bound is equality at $z=0$.

By the definitions, $\mathcal L_c(v)+mc^2-\mathcal L_N(v)=-mc^2(f(z)-1+z/2)=-mc^2q(z)$. Step 1.2 and $z^2\le C^4\varepsilon^2$ give the asserted action-density bound. On a fixed interval $[a,b]$, integrating the subtracted constant $mc^2$ contributes $mc^2(b-a)$, independent of the path, so it does not change fixed-endpoint stationary variations.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and step 1.1 quantify conditionally over individual stipulated speed data with positive epsilon and rho<1. There is no sum over a family; an empty selection of admissible states makes the universal estimate vacuous. The allowed v=0 state is checked separately in step 1.2.
Step 1.2 and step 2.1 give equality for v=0.

boundaries.reason: No counting or one-element selection claim occurs.

boundaries.evidence: At z=0 the pointwise remainders and the action-density difference vanish by steps 1.2 and 2.1.
The endpoint epsilon=epsilon_* gives z<=rho<1 in step 1.1; step 1.2 bounds the action remainder on [0,rho].

boundaries.reason: The proof is pointwise for every family member and invokes no selection principle.

Statement — Uniform low-speed relativistic remainders: These conditional identities or constructions do not assert an additional biconditional beyond their stated formulation. Positive epsilon with C squared epsilon_* below one bounds every stipulated speed state by a common rho<1. Zero velocity is allowed and the square-root remainder is exact there; the estimates are pointwise uniform over members, with no nonempty aggregate or trajectory claim.

Statement — Uniform low-speed relativistic remainders: No reverse implication from an observed or formal output to a broader model or unspecified input is asserted. Positive epsilon with C squared epsilon_* below one bounds every stipulated speed state by a common rho<1. Zero velocity is allowed and the square-root remainder is exact there; the estimates are pointwise uniform over members, with no nonempty aggregate or trajectory claim.

finite_checks.check: Set v=0 for any 0<epsilon<=epsilon_*.
finite_checks.result: All momentum, energy and action-density remainders vanish exactly.
finite_checks.verifies: The z=0 branch in step 1.2 and the identity in step 2.1.

finite_checks.check: Set epsilon=epsilon_* and |v|=C sqrt(epsilon_*) c when this saturates the family cutoff.
finite_checks.result: Then z=rho<1; the denominators remain positive and the uniform estimates retain their stated finite constants.
finite_checks.verifies: The endpoint substitution in steps 1.1 and 1.2.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space of dimension four with signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and fix an inertial chart $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ with $x^0=ct$, $c>0$. Let $O\subseteq A$ be open and let $F$ be a $C^2$ alternating covariant two-tensor on $O$. In this chart write $F^a{}_b:=\eta^{ac}F_{cb}$ and let $\partial_b$ denote the coordinate partial derivative. Fix constants $\alpha\in\mathbb R$ and $\tau_e\geq0$. For every $U\in V$, define

$$\Pi_U{}^a{}_b:=\delta^a_b+\frac{U^aU_b}{c^2},\qquad f_0^a(x,U):=\alpha F^a{}_b(x)U^b,$$

$$B^a(x,U):=\alpha(\partial_bF^a{}_c)(x)U^bU^c +\alpha^2F^a{}_b(x)F^b{}_c(x)U^c, \qquad a_{\rm LL}^a(x,U):=f_0^a(x,U)+\tau_e\Pi_U{}^a{}_bB^b(x,U).$$

For the physical interpretation, $x^a$ are in metres, $\tau$ is in seconds, $c$ is in metres per second, $U$ is in metres per second, $\alpha=q/m$, and $\tau_e$ is a time. Here a **proper-time parameter** means that the parameter is measured in seconds and the four-velocity is normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$; define the future unit shell by $\mathcal S^+:=\{U\in C^+:\eta(U,U)=-c^2\}$. For each initial datum $(x_0,U_0)\in O\times V$ with $U_0\in\mathcal S^+$, the system

$$\frac{dx^a}{d\tau}=U^a,\qquad \frac{dU^a}{d\tau}=a_{\rm LL}^a(x,U),\qquad (x(0),U(0))=(x_0,U_0)$$

has a unique local solution on an open proper-time interval about $0$. Along that interval $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ remains future directed. This is a local ODE statement: it makes no claim of global existence for arbitrary $F$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: Differentiating $\eta(U_\varepsilon,U_\varepsilon)=-c^2$ gives $\eta(U_\varepsilon,a_\varepsilon)=0$. Differentiating this identity once more gives $\eta(U_\varepsilon,\dot a_\varepsilon)=-\eta(a_\varepsilon,a_\varepsilon)$. By [F1], $\Pi_{U_\varepsilon}\dot a_\varepsilon=\dot a_\varepsilon+U_\varepsilon\eta(U_\varepsilon,\dot a_\varepsilon)/c^2=\dot a_\varepsilon-\eta(a_\varepsilon,a_\varepsilon)U_\varepsilon/c^2$. Therefore [A1] is exactly $a_\varepsilon=f_{0,\varepsilon}+\varepsilon\Pi_{U_\varepsilon}\dot a_\varepsilon$.

The product and chain rules [F2], with $\dot x=U$ and $\dot U=a$, give $$\dot f_{0,\varepsilon}^a=\alpha_\varepsilon(\partial_bF^a{}_c)U^bU^c+\alpha_\varepsilon F^a{}_b a_\varepsilon^b, \qquad B_\varepsilon^a=\alpha_\varepsilon(\partial_bF^a{}_c)U^bU^c+\alpha_\varepsilon F^a{}_b f_{0,\varepsilon}^b.$$ Subtracting the equalities and using $\delta_\varepsilon=a_\varepsilon-f_{0,\varepsilon}$ gives $\dot f_{0,\varepsilon}-B_\varepsilon=\alpha_\varepsilon F\delta_\varepsilon$.

Subtract $f_{0,\varepsilon}+\varepsilon\Pi_{U_\varepsilon}B_\varepsilon$ from the reformulated LAD equation in step 1.1. Since $\dot a-B=\dot\delta+(\dot f_0-B)$, step 2.1 yields $$a_\varepsilon-(f_{0,\varepsilon}+\varepsilon\Pi_{U_\varepsilon}B_\varepsilon) =\varepsilon\Pi_{U_\varepsilon}(\dot\delta_\varepsilon+\alpha_\varepsilon F\delta_\varepsilon).$$ Taking Euclidean norms and applying the assumed bounds gives at each $\tau\in I$ $$\left\|a_\varepsilon-(f_{0,\varepsilon}+\varepsilon\Pi_{U_\varepsilon}B_\varepsilon)\right\| \leq\varepsilon P(C_1\varepsilon+A M C_0\varepsilon) =P(C_1+AM C_0)\varepsilon^2.$$ The constants do not depend on $\varepsilon$ or $\tau$, so the estimate is uniform on $I$.

boundaries.evidence: Step 3.1 states the pointwise estimate, which is vacuous if the common interval has no points.
Step 3.1 remains valid when any bound constant is zero; epsilon itself is positive.

boundaries.reason: No singleton family or one-index boundary occurs in the uniform estimate.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.1–3.1 require no invertibility or nondegeneracy beyond c>0 and the normalized shell.
Step 3.1 is pointwise on the closed common interval, so its endpoints are included under the stated uniform bounds.
Step 3.1 is pointwise for the given family and uses no choice principle.

Positive epsilon labels C3 LAD curves on one nondegenerate compact interval, with uniform defect and derivative bounds assumed. The resulting quadratic residual estimate neither constructs those curves nor establishes global convergence.
