citations.quote:
This item assumes the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through
the tangent-bundle structure used by
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (c)
([[def-countable-choice]]); no further choice principle is used.

**(a) Parameters and the Schwarzschild radius.** Let $c>0$ and $G_N>0$ be real
constants and let $m_*>0$ be a real **mass parameter**. Put

$$s:=\frac{2G_Nm_*}{c^2}>0 .$$

The number $s$ is the **Schwarzschild radius** of the datum. Neither $c$,
$G_N$ nor $m_*$ is measured here; the physical reading of $c$ and $G_N$ as the
framework's conversion and Newton constants and of $m_*$ as a mass is fixed by
the physical conventions of the framework, not by this definition.

**(b) The underlying manifold and its product charts.** Let $S^2:=S_2(0,1)=
\{y\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert y\rVert_2=1\}$ be the unit Euclidean sphere with the
subspace topology of [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]. Specify its
smooth structure as the maximal atlas generated by the following two charts
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). For $\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}$ put
$p_\varepsilon=(0,0,\varepsilon)$ and
$U_\varepsilon=S^2\setminus\{p_\varepsilon\}$, and define

$$\sigma_\varepsilon:U_\varepsilon\to\mathbb R^2,\qquad \sigma_\varepsilon(y)=\frac{(y_1,y_2)}{1-\varepsilon y_3}.$$

These open domains cover $S^2$. Each chart is a homeomorphism onto
$\mathbb R^2$, with inverse, for $u=(u_1,u_2)$ and $q=u_1^2+u_2^2$,

$$\sigma_\varepsilon^{-1}(u)=\left(\frac{2u_1}{1+q},\frac{2u_2}{1+q},\varepsilon\frac{q-1}{1+q}\right).$$

The two inverse identities follow by substitution; all displayed denominators
are nonzero on their domains. On the overlap both transition maps are
$u\mapsto u/(u_1^2+u_2^2)$ on $\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$, hence smooth.
The subspace is Hausdorff and has a countable basis given by intersections
with Euclidean balls of rational centres and positive rational radii.
Thus these charts specify a smooth two-manifold without boundary. This is
the standard sphere structure used for the round metric below: the inclusion
has the displayed smooth local parametrizations, and their differentials
are injective because composition with $\sigma_\varepsilon$ is the identity.
Let $M$ be the product manifold

$$M:=\mathbb R\times(s,\infty)\times S^2$$

with the product smooth structure
([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]]);
it is a smooth four-manifold without boundary. Write $x^0:M\to\mathbb R$ and
$r:M\to(s,\infty)$ for the first and second projections and $\iota:M\to S^2$
for the third. A **product chart** of $M$ is a smooth chart on the product
whose angular part is a smooth chart of $S^2$. In a **spherical-polar product
chart**, $0<\vartheta<\pi$ and the components of the round metric
$\gamma_{S^2}$ of [[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]
are $\gamma_{22}=1$, $\gamma_{23}=\gamma_{32}=0$,
$\gamma_{33}=\sin^2\vartheta$. These polar charts omit the two poles; ordinary
smooth sphere charts around the poles complete the product atlas.

**(c) The metric.** Let $f:(s,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ be the smooth function

$$f(r):=1-\frac{s}{r} .$$

Define $g$ globally by the coordinate-free expression

$$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In every spherical-polar product chart its component functions are

$$g_{00}:=-f(r),\qquad g_{11}:=\frac{1}{f(r)},\qquad g_{22}:=r^2,\qquad g_{33}:=r^2\sin^2\vartheta,$$

and $g_{ab}:=0$ whenever $a\ne b$, $a,b\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, with the index order
$(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)=(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$. This is a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field on all of $M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]); the component display is local
to spherical-polar charts, and $f>0$ because $r>s$. The pair $(M,g)$ is the **Schwarzschild exterior
metric of mass parameter $m_*$**; the datum of this definition is the
quadruple $(c,G_N,m_*,g)$. With these parameters fixed, write $(M,g,N)$
for its associated geometric datum, with $N$ as in clause (d). The geometric
datum depends on the parameters only through $s$ and does not retain $c$,
$G_N$ and $m_*$ separately. That $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ is not asserted here; it is proved in the companion metric-properties lemma of this page (its
justification record in the frontmatter), which also records the equivalent
coordinate-free description
$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}$.

**(d) Time orientation and the Schwarzschild chart.** The field
$N:=\partial_0$ is the smooth product vector field on $M$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); the chart components of $g$
are independent of $x^0$, so $N$ is the restriction of a global vector field,
and $g(N,N)=-f(r)<0$ at every point. The datum carries the time orientation
$N$. Spherical-polar product charts are **Schwarzschild charts** of the datum;
at the poles the same metric is represented in the smooth sphere charts of
the product atlas. We write $t$ for the coordinate $x^0/c$ when the datum is
read in the framework's unit conventions.

**(e) Scope.** The domain of the datum is the exterior region $r>s$; the
definition asserts nothing about $r=s$, about $r\le 0$, about any matter, or
about any equation satisfied by $g$. The horizon $r=s$ is not part of the
datum, and a continuation of the metric to $r=s$ requires the separate constructions recorded on this page, the
regularity lemma for the advanced chart and the Kruskal model-properties
lemma. Whether the datum is a solution of the
framework's field law is proved, not defined, in the Ricci-and-Einstein-tensor lemma of this
page.

Let $c>0$, $G_N>0$, $m_*>0$ and let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior
datum of mass parameter $m_*$ with Schwarzschild radius
$s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]). Then:

**(a) Global metric and local components.** $M$ is a smooth four-manifold
without boundary and $g$ is the smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field
globally defined by

$$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In every spherical-polar product chart $(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ its
components are

$$g_{00}=-f(r),\qquad g_{11}=\frac{1}{f(r)},\qquad g_{22}=r^2,\qquad g_{33}=r^2\sin^2\vartheta,\qquad g_{ab}=0\ (a\ne b),$$

where $f(r)=1-s/r$, $\iota:M\to S^2$ is the third projection and
$\gamma_{S^2}$ is the round metric of the unit sphere. The component display
is local to the spherical-polar charts; the global tensor formula includes
the poles.

**(b) Lorentzian signature.** At every $p\in M$ the form $g_p$ is
nondegenerate with inertia $(3,1,0)$; consequently $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth
Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$.

**(c) Time orientation.** The global product field $N=\partial_0$ is smooth
and nowhere vanishing, and $g_p(N_p,N_p)=-f(r(p))<0$ at every $p$; it is
therefore a time orientation of $(M,g)$. The globally defined base fields
$\partial_0,\partial_r$ are orthogonal with squared norms $-f$ and $f^{-1}$.
In a spherical-polar chart the angular coordinate fields are orthogonal with
positive squared norms $r^2$ and $r^2\sin^2\vartheta$; at a pole use any
angular chart and the positive-definite round metric instead.

**(d) Domain of the coordinates.** Product charts form an atlas covering
$M$. Spherical-polar charts are defined on the regular angular locus
$0<\vartheta<\pi$ and omit the poles; pole charts are ordinary smooth charts
of $S^2$. The functions $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are smooth on $r>s$, and the
spherical-polar component functions are smooth on their chart domains.

**(e) Conventions.** The global tensor identity holds on all of $M$; the
displayed component identities are in spherical-polar product charts. In pole
charts the sphere block is $r^2$ times the round-metric component matrix.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\nabla$ be an affine connection
on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]). Smooth vector fields
are smooth sections of the tangent bundle
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]); as there, their use
rests on the canonical smooth structure of $TM$, which assumes the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]]. This is the only use of that
axiom in this definition.

**(a) Metric compatibility.** The connection $\nabla$ is **$g$-compatible**, or
**compatible with the metric** $g$, when for all smooth vector fields $X,Y,Z$ on
$M$ the identity of smooth functions

$$X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$$

holds on $M$. Here $g(Y,Z)$ is the smooth function $p\mapsto g_p(Y_p,Z_p)$ and
$X$ acts on functions as a derivation; the identity uses only the action of
$\nabla$ on vector fields and requires no extension of $\nabla$ to tensor
fields. When such an extension is available, this identity is the statement
$\nabla_Xg=0$, and the compatibility of $\nabla$ with the inverse metric
$g^{-1}$ follows; neither statement is part of this definition.

**(b) Torsion freedom.** The **torsion** of $\nabla$ is the tangent-valued
$2$-tensor $T(X,Y)=\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX-[X,Y]$ of
[[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]], with bracket as in
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]. The connection is **torsion-free**
when $T(X,Y)=0$ for all smooth $X,Y$, that is, when
$\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$ identically.

**(c) Metric-selected connections.** A **metric-selected connection** for
$(M,g)$ is an affine connection on $M$ that is both torsion-free and
$g$-compatible. Equivalently, it is an element of the class

$$\operatorname{LC}(M,g):=\{\nabla:\nabla\text{ is an affine connection on }M,\ \nabla\text{ is torsion-free and }g\text{-compatible}\}.$$

The name records that the pair of conditions selects the connection out of all
affine connections; it is the pair of conditions imposed on the connection that
conventional general relativity uses, and the connection so selected is called
the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.


**(d) Intrinsic construction before physical use.** For smooth local vector
fields define the Koszul expression

$$K(X,Y,Z):=Xg(Y,Z)+Yg(Z,X)-Zg(X,Y)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X).$$

Define $\nabla^g_XY$ by $2g(\nabla^g_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)$ for every smooth local
$Z$. The proof below establishes existence, smoothness, the affine-connection
rules, metric compatibility, torsion freedom and uniqueness; it uses symmetry
and nondegeneracy, not positive definiteness. Thus $\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$
has this unique element, called the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$. The later
nondegenerate-metric theorem retains its fuller tensor-derivative statement.
Its Christoffel symbols in any chart are defined by
$\nabla^g_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]) and obey

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12 g^{ad}(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}),\qquad a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3.$$

**(e) Basic curvature and contractions.** The **curvature** of this connection
is the operator of [[def-curvature-of-an-affine-connection]], with the fixed
sign convention

$$R^g(X,Y)Z:=\nabla^g_X\nabla^g_YZ-\nabla^g_Y\nabla^g_XZ-\nabla^g_{[X,Y]}Z.$$

The general affine-connection theorem
[[thm-curvature-is-a-type-one-three-tensor]] proves that it depends pointwise
only on $X,Y,Z$ and is a smooth tensor. Define its chart components by
$R^g(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=R^a{}_{bcd}\partial_a$.
Define the **Ricci tensor** and **scalar curvature** pointwise by

$$\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,w):=\operatorname{tr}(z\mapsto R^g_p(z,w)v),\qquad S(p):=\operatorname{tr}(\sharp_p\circ\operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p),\qquad \operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p(v):=\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,\cdot).$$

Here $\sharp$ is the inverse metric isomorphism and traces are the
basis-independent trace of [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. Equivalently,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}=\sum_aR^a{}_{bad}$ and
$S=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}$, all sums from $0$ through $3$.
These are well-defined smooth fields by finite contraction of the smooth
components of $R^g$ and $g^{-1}$; basis independence follows from the trace
and the intrinsic maps just defined. No symmetry identity or field equation
is assumed here. Lowering the curvature output gives
$R_{abcd}=g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd}$, so the definitions agree with the full later
curvature item, which proves the remaining symmetries and coordinate formulas.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be an oriented time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]).

**(a) Characterization of Killing fields.** For every smooth vector field
$\xi$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]), with
$\xi_b=g_{bc}\xi^c$ the lowered field,

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nabla_a\xi_b+\nabla_b\xi_a=0 .$$

**(b) Contraction along geodesics.** If $\xi$ is a Killing field and
$\gamma:I\to M$ is a geodesic with $D_t\gamma'=0$ in its affine parameter
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]), then $t\mapsto
g_{\gamma(t)}(\xi_{\gamma(t)},\gamma'(t))$ is constant on $I$.

**(c) Conserved current.** Let $U\subseteq M$ be open, let $T$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $U$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) with
$\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$ on $U$, and let $\xi$ be a Killing field on $U$. Then
$J^{a}:=T^{ab}\xi_b$ is a smooth vector field on $U$ with
$\nabla_aJ^a=0$; consequently the flux balance of
[[thm-gr-density-divergence-and-finite-chain-flux]] clause (b) applies to $J$
on every smooth singular $4$-chain contained in $U$.

**(d) On-shell conservation of the Hilbert tensor.** Let $c>0$, let
$S:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R$ be a model action with Hilbert stress-energy tensor
$T$ at $(g,\varphi)$ with respect to $c$
([[def-gr-hilbert-stress-energy-tensor]]). For the flow diffeomorphisms $F$
below, suppose the configuration set $\mathcal X$ carries specified maps
$P_F:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X$ with $P_{\mathrm{id}}=\mathrm{id}$; write
$F^*\varphi:=P_F(\varphi)$. For geometric matter fields these are the
model's pullbacks; no pullback operation on an arbitrary set is implicit.
For **every** smooth compactly supported vector field $\xi$, its flow
$\Phi_v$ is global
([[def-complete-vector-field]], [[def-local-and-global-flow]]); this holds for
every compactly supported smooth field, using the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]] through
[[thm-compactly-supported-vector-fields-are-complete]]. Write
$G(u,v):=S(\Phi_v^*g,\Phi_u^*\varphi)$ for the simultaneous pullback by the
flow (this presupposes that the pairs lie in $\mathcal D$, which is part of the
hypotheses below). Suppose (H1)–(H4) hold for **every** such $\xi$ (with
its own $G$ and parameter neighborhood):

- **(H1)** the map $G$ is defined on a neighborhood of $(0,0)$ in
  $\mathbb R^2$ and is differentiable at $(0,0)$;
- **(H2)** $\partial_uG(0,0)=0$ (the matter configuration $\varphi$ satisfies
  its model equations in this direction);
- **(H3)** $\partial_vG(0,0)=-\frac{1}{2c}\int_MT_{ab}q^{ab}\mathrm{vol}_g$,
  where $q^{ab}:=\partial_v(\Phi_v^*g)^{ab}|_{v=0}$ (the metric variation is
  represented by the Hilbert tensor);
- **(H4)** $G(s,s)=S(g,\varphi)$ whenever $(s,s)$ lies in that neighborhood
  (invariance of the action under simultaneous pullback by the flow).

Then $\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$ on $M$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\xi$ be a smooth vector field
on $M$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). The **Lie
derivative of the metric along $\xi$**, written $\mathcal L_\xi g$, is the
smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field obtained by the flow definition of
[[def-lie-derivative-of-a-tensor-field]] applied to $g$: for the local flow
$\Phi_t$ of $\xi$,

$$\mathcal L_\xi g:=\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\Phi_t^*g .$$

The field $\xi$ is a **Killing field** of $(M,g)$ (an **isometry generator**,
or a **Killing vector**) when

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0 .$$

The equivalent local characterization

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nabla_a\xi_b+\nabla_b\xi_a=0,$$

where $\nabla$ is the metric-selected connection of $g$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and
$\xi_b:=g_{bc}\xi^c$ is the lowered field, is proved in
[[thm-gr-killing-and-on-shell-matter-identities]] clause (a); the definition
itself asserts neither direction. Whether a given metric has Killing fields is
a property of that metric: neither existence nor uniqueness of a Killing field
is asserted here, and a general metric has none beyond the trivial field
$\xi=0$.

If $X$ has local flow $\Phi_t$ and $T$ is a smooth tensor field of type $(r,s)$, its Lie derivative is $$\mathcal L_XT=\left.\frac d{dt}\right|_{t=0}\Phi_t^*T,$$ on every local flow domain where this derivative is defined. Here the pullback by the local diffeomorphism $\Phi_t$ acts by $d\Phi_{-t}$ on each contravariant slot and by $d\Phi_t$ on each covariant slot.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold without boundary with affine connection $\nabla$, and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior. A smooth curve $\gamma:I\to M$ is an **affinely parametrized geodesic** when
$$D_t\gamma'(t)=0\qquad(t\in I),$$
with one-sided interpretation at an included endpoint. Constant curves are geodesics. Unless another parametrization is explicitly stated, “geodesic” means affinely parametrized geodesic.

derivations.claim: In each equatorial spherical chart the components in [F1] are independent of $x^0$ and $\varphi$, and the coordinate components of $\partial_0$ and the axial generator $\partial_\varphi$ are constant. The flow pullback derivative in [F2] therefore gives $\mathcal L_{\partial_0}g=\mathcal L_{\partial_\varphi}g=0$, so both fields are locally Killing. By the conservation part of [F2] and the affine geodesic equation [F3], $-g(\partial_0,\gamma')=f\,dx^0/d\lambda=E$ and $g(\partial_\varphi,\gamma')=r^2d\varphi/d\lambda=L$ are constant on each chart interval; longitude charts differ by additive constants, so these values agree on overlaps and are constant along $\gamma$.

At $\vartheta=\pi/2$, the null condition and [F1] give $0=-f\left(\frac{dx^0}{d\lambda}\right)^2+f^{-1}\left(\frac{dr}{d\lambda}\right)^2+r^2\left(\frac{d\varphi}{d\lambda}\right)^2.$ Substitute $dx^0/d\lambda=E/f$ and $d\varphi/d\lambda=L/r^2$, then multiply by $f>0$. The result is $(dr/d\lambda)^2=E^2[1-(L/E)^2f/r^2]$, the asserted radial first integral.

Differentiating $H(r)=r^{-2}-sr^{-3}$ yields $H'(r)=-2r^{-3}+3sr^{-4}=(3s-2r)/r^4$. Since $r^4>0$, this derivative is positive on $(s,3s/2)$ and negative on $(3s/2,\infty)$; hence the unique maximum is at $3s/2$. Substitution gives $H(3s/2)=4/(27s^2)$, and solving $b^2H(3s/2)=1$ gives $b_{\rm c}=3\sqrt3s/2$.

The right side of the radial first integral vanishes at a radius precisely when $b^2H(r)=1$. Since $H$ is positive on $r>s$, tends to zero at both ends, and has the maximum computed in the preceding step, the threshold for the existence of an exterior root is exactly $b_{\rm c}$. This is a first-integral statement only; it asserts no global scattering continuation.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Fix $x\ne0$. By [F1] and [F2], sine is continuous on the closed interval with endpoints $0,x$ and differentiable in its interior. By [F3] there is $\xi_x$ strictly between $0$ and $x$ such that $\sin x/x=(\sin x-\sin0)/(x-0)=\cos\xi_x$.

Given $\varepsilon>0$, [F1] and [F2] make cosine continuous at $0$, so choose $\delta>0$ such that $|t|<\delta$ implies $|\cos t-1|<\varepsilon$. If $0<|x|<\delta$, then $|\xi_x|<|x|<\delta$ and step 1.1 yields $|\sin x/x-1|=|\cos\xi_x-1|<\varepsilon$. This is the stated limit.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

**(f) Scope.** Proper time, length and four-velocity are defined only for
future timelike worldlines. A null or spacelike curve receives no proper time
and no four-velocity from this definition, and no limiting or distributional
extension of the square-root integrand to such curves is asserted. The
parametrization of a worldline is part of the data and is arbitrary in this
definition: no affine parameter, no geodesic equation, no completeness or
extendability of the domain, and no measurement or clock reading is assumed.
Null and spacelike regularity classes are not defined here beyond the general
$C^k$ and piecewise-$C^1$ notions of clause (a), which make no causal
requirement.

For a given connection on $E$ and a smooth curve on an interval with nonempty interior, the **covariant derivative along the curve** is
$$D_tV=(\gamma^*\nabla)_{\partial/\partial t}V.$$
Here $V$ is a section of the pullback bundle as in [[def-vector-field-and-section-along-a-smooth-curve]], and the pullback connection exists by [[thm-pullback-connection-is-well-defined-and-functorial]]. It is real-linear and satisfies $D_t(fV)=f'V+fD_tV$ for functions of the parameter.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let
$R$, $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ be as in
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. Then the following
identities hold for all indices $a,b,c,d\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ and at every point of
every smooth chart:

1. If $w$ is nonzero future causal, then $\gamma(w)>0$.
2. If $w$ is future unit timelike, then $\gamma(w)\ge1$, with
   $\gamma(w)=1$ if and only if $w=n$, and
   $g_p(h(w),h(w))=\gamma(w)^2-1$.
3. If $w$ is unit timelike, then $w$ is future-directed if and only if
   $g_p(n,w)<0$, and past-directed if and only if $g_p(n,w)>0$; in particular
   $g_p(n,w)\neq0$ for such $w$.

Assume Countable Choice as inherited by the supplied Lorentzian smooth-structure and connection results. Let $z:I\to M$ be a $C^2$ future timelike worldline in a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$, parametrized by proper time, with $U=D_\tau z$ and $g(U,U)=-c^2$. Let $p$ be a $C^1$ vector field along $z$, let $S^{ab}=-S^{ba}$ and $\mathcal T^{ab}=-\mathcal T^{ba}$ be $C^1$ bivector fields along $z$, and let $n$ be a $C^1$ future unit timelike field along $z$. Suppose
$$S^{ab}n_b=0,\qquad D_\tau S^{ab}=p^aU^b-p^bU^a+\mathcal T^{ab}.$$
Define $\gamma:=-g(n,U)/c$ and $E_n:=-c\,g(p,n)$. Then $\gamma>0$, and
$$c\gamma\,p^a=\frac{E_n}{c}U^a+S^{ab}D_\tau n_b+\mathcal T^{ab}n_b.$$
Here $\mathcal T$ denotes an arbitrary antisymmetric torque; setting it to zero gives the torque-free case.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\nabla$ be an affine connection
on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]). Smooth vector fields
are smooth sections of the tangent bundle
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]); as there, their use
rests on the canonical smooth structure of $TM$, which assumes the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]]. This is the only use of that
axiom in this definition.

derivations.claim: Under [A2]'s TD condition $C=0$, take $n=p/\mu$. Then $n$ is a future unit observer, $S^{ab}n_b=0$, $\gamma=-g(p,U)/(\mu c)=mc/\mu$, and $E_n=-cg(p,p/\mu)=c\mu$. Also $D_\tau n=D_\tau p/\mu-p\,D_\tau\mu/\mu^2$; contracting with $S$ removes the second term because $S^{ab}p_b=0$. Substitution in [F4] and multiplication by $\mu$ give $mc^2p=\mu^2U+S f$. The definition of $f$ in (1) now gives exactly $KU=mc^2p$. Positivity of $m$ follows from [F3].

Since $K$ is invertible, step 1.1 gives $U=mc^2W$. The coefficient is positive, so $W$ is future timelike. Its normalization is $-c^2=g(U,U)=m^2c^4g(W,W)$, hence $m=1/(c\sqrt{-g(W,W)})$ and the second formula in (2) follows. Conversely, on $C=0$, contraction of $K^a{}_b$ with $p_a$ gives $p_aK^a{}_b=\mu^2p_b$ because $p_aS^{ac}=-C^c=0$. Multiplying by $W^b$ yields $g(p,W)=-1$, so the normalized formula has $m=-g(p,U)/c^2=1/(c\sqrt{-g(W,W)})$ and satisfies the first formula in (2).

On the open region stated in the theorem, the inverse $K^{-1}$ and the positive square root $\sqrt{-g(W,W)}$ depend smoothly on the state coordinates. The smooth Lorentzian background, curvature and metric-selected connection [F2, F6] make the coordinate form of $z'=U$, (1) a smooth, hence locally Lipschitz, vector field. [F5] gives unique local solutions. For constraint preservation, set $\lambda:=c/\sqrt{-g(W,W)}$, so $KU=\lambda p$ throughout this open region. The product rule [F1] gives
$$D_\tau C^a=p^a g(p,U)+\mu^2U^a+S^{ab}f_b=p^a(g(p,U)+\lambda).$$
Moreover, $p_aK^a{}_bU^b=\mu^2g(p,U)-C^bf_b=\lambda g(p,p)=-\lambda\mu^2$, so $\mu^2(g(p,U)+\lambda)=C^bf_b$. Therefore
$$D_\tau C^a=\frac{p^a f_b}{\mu^2}C^b.$$
This is a homogeneous linear ODE for $C$ along the solution. Its unique solution with $C(\tau_0)=0$ is $C\equiv0$, proving preservation.

On the preserved constraint, step 1.1 gives $\mu^2U=mc^2p-Sf$. The curvature antisymmetry [F2] yields $g(U,f)=-\tfrac12R_{abcd}U^aU^bS^{cd}=0$. Contract the displayed relation with $f_a$: the left side is zero and $f_aS^{ab}f_b=0$ by antisymmetry of $S$, so $mc^2g(p,f)=0$. Since step 1.1 gives $m>0$ and $c>0$, $g(p,f)=0$, hence $D_\tau g(p,p)=2g(p,f)=0$ and $\mu$ is constant. Also
$$\frac12D_\tau(S_{ab}S^{ab})=S_{ab}(p^aU^b-p^bU^a)=2S_{ab}p^aU^b=0$$
by $C=0$ from step 3.1.

If $S=0$, then $f=0$, $K=\mu^2\operatorname{Id}$, and $W=p/\mu^2$ with $g(W,W)=-1/\mu^2$. The normalized formula (2) gives $U=cp/\mu$, equivalently $p=(\mu/c)U$. Equation (1) gives $D_\tau p=0$; since $\mu$ is constant by step 4.1, $D_\tau U=0$.

Let $m,c,\kappa>0$, let $x,p\in\mathbb R^3$, and set

$$D:=(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb R^3,\qquad r:=|x|,\qquad \mathcal E(p):=\sqrt{m^2c^4+c^2|p|^2}.$$

The **repulsive relativistic Coulomb Hamiltonian** is

$$H(x,p):=\mathcal E(p)+\frac{\kappa}{r},$$

and its **phase system** is the autonomous ODE on the open set $D$

$$\dot x=\nabla_pH=\frac{c^2p}{\mathcal E(p)},\qquad \dot p=-\nabla_xH=\frac{\kappa x}{r^3}.$$

Here the system parameter $t$ is time in seconds and dot denotes $d/dt$; $m$ is a positive mass parameter (kilograms in the SI interpretation), $c$ a positive speed parameter (metres per second), and $\kappa$ a positive energy-times-length parameter (joule-metres). Define the radial momentum $p_r:=x\cdot p/r$ and angular-momentum vector $J:=x\times p$. A trajectory is a $C^1$ solution of this ODE on an interval; maximality is in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]].

This is only a mathematical phase system. Its physical interpretation as a charged particle in an externally prescribed Coulomb field requires separate model assumptions.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniformly in time, in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]. Let $t_0<b$ be reals, let $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$ with $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, and let $x:[t_0,b)\to\mathbb R^n$ be a solution of the initial value problem

$$x'(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),\qquad x(t_0)=x_0$$

on $[t_0,b)$ ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]). Suppose there is a compact set $K\subseteq D$ and a real $\delta>0$ such that

$$\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)\in K\qquad\text{for every }t\in(b-\delta,b)\cap[t_0,b).$$

Then:

1. there is $\varepsilon>0$ and a solution $\tilde x:[t_0,b+\varepsilon)\to\mathbb R^n$ of the same initial value problem with $\tilde x(t)=x(t)$ for all $t\in[t_0,b)$; in particular $\tilde x(b)=\lim_{t\uparrow b}x(t)$ exists and lies in the state projection of $K$;
2. if moreover $D=\mathbb R\times U$ for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $F$ is autonomous, $F(t,z)=G(z)$ with $G:U\to\mathbb R^n$ continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]), and if there is a compact $K_0\subseteq U$ with $x(t)\in K_0$ for every $t\in(b-\delta,b)\cap[t_0,b)$, then the extension conclusion of clause 1 holds as well.

By [[lem-tangent-principal-branch-is-bijective]], tangent restricts to a
continuous strictly increasing bijection

$$\tan:(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\longrightarrow\mathbb R.$$

Its inverse is the **principal inverse tangent**

$$\arctan:\mathbb R\longrightarrow(-\pi/2,\pi/2).$$

Thus $\tan(\arctan y)=y$ for every real $y$, while
$\arctan(\tan x)=x$ precisely for $x$ in the displayed principal interval.
The inverse is continuous and strictly increasing by [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

The restriction

$$\tan:(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\longrightarrow\mathbb R$$

is continuous, strictly increasing, and bijective.

Sine is differentiable, hence continuous, and strictly increasing on
$[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$; its endpoint values are $-1$ and $1$
([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]],
[[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]],
[[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]],
[[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]). The intermediate value
theorem therefore makes its restricted image exactly $[-1,1]$
([[thm-intermediate-value]]). Likewise, cosine is continuous and strictly
decreasing on $[0,\pi]$, with endpoint values $1$ and $-1$, so its restricted
image is $[-1,1]$ ([[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]],
[[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[thm-intermediate-value]]).
Their principal inverses are denoted

$$\arcsin:[-1,1]\to[-\pi/2,\pi/2],\qquad\arccos:[-1,1]\to[0,\pi],$$

and are characterised by

$$\sin(\arcsin y)=y,\qquad\cos(\arccos y)=y\qquad(-1\le y\le1).$$

The chosen target intervals are part of the notation: without them, inverse
sine and inverse cosine would be multivalued relations rather than functions.
Their continuity follows from [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]), let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and injective
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), and let $g : f[I] \to I$ be the
inverse of $f : I \to f[I]$ supplied by [[thm-continuous-inverse]]. Let
$c \in I$ and put $b := f(c)$.

Then $c$ is a limit point of $I$ and $b$ is a limit point of $f[I]$, so that
$f'(c)$ and $g'(b)$ are meaningful symbols ([[def-derivative]]), and, assuming
$f$ is differentiable at $c$:

1. if $f'(c) \ne 0$, then $g$ is differentiable at $b$ and
   $$g'(b) \;=\; \frac{1}{f'(c)} ;$$
2. if $f'(c) = 0$, then $g$ is **not** differentiable at $b$.

**The two claims together say that the inverse inherits differentiability
exactly where the derivative does not vanish.** Nothing is asserted at a point
of $f[I]$ that is not of the form $f(c)$ with $f$ differentiable at $c$, and
nothing is asserted about $g$ being differentiable *on* a set.

**No compactness and no boundedness is assumed.** $I$ may be open, half-open or
unbounded; all that is used of it is order-convexity and the presence of two
distinct points, the latter being exactly what makes every point of $I$ a limit
point of $I$ ([[def-derivative]]).

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$, $\sin ^2x+\cos ^2x=1$, $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$, and $\cos(-x)=\cos x$. Wherever the displayed quotients are defined, $\tan(-x)=-\tan x$, $\cot(-x)=-\cot x$, $\sec(-x)=\sec x$, $\csc(-x)=-\csc x$, $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$, and $1+\cot^2x=\csc^2x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]), let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]). The words
*nondecreasing*, *increasing*, *nonincreasing* and *decreasing* are those of
[[def-monotone-function]], in which *increasing* is the strict notion.

1. If $f'(x) \ge 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is
   nondecreasing on $I$.
2. If $f'(x) > 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is increasing on
   $I$.
3. If $f'(x) \le 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is
   nonincreasing on $I$.
4. If $f'(x) < 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is decreasing on
   $I$.

Conversely, with no continuity hypothesis and no hypothesis at any other point:

5. If $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ is nondecreasing on $I$ and differentiable at a
   point $c \in I$ that is a limit point of $I$, then $f'(c) \ge 0$; if $f$ is
   nonincreasing and differentiable at such a $c$, then $f'(c) \le 0$.

**No strict converse is claimed here, and none is true.** Claim 5 gives the
weak inequality only, and it cannot be improved: an increasing function may have
a vanishing derivative at a point. That failure is recorded separately, as a
false statement later on this page, with its witness worked out on the companion
page. Reading claim 2 backwards is the single most common misuse of this
theorem, and this statement does not license it.

**Claims 1 to 4 need the interval; claim 5 does not.** The forward direction
runs through the mean value theorem on a segment joining two points of $I$, so
order-convexity is essential. Claim 5 is a statement about one point and uses
only that the difference quotients have a constant sign.

The limit over nonzero real $x$ is

$$\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1.$$

Along any solution of [F1], $\dot H=
abla_xH\cdot\dot x+
abla_pH\cdot\dot p=
abla_xH\cdot
abla_pH-
abla_pH\cdot
abla_xH=0,$ and $\dot J=\dot x	imes p+x	imes\dot p=0$ because $\dot x$ is parallel to $p$ and $\dot p$ is parallel to $x$. Thus $W$ and $J$ are constant. With $u=1/r$, the energy relation gives $\mathcal E=W-\kappa u$, so $c^2|p|^2=(W-\kappa u)^2-m^2c^4,$ and $|p|^2=p_r^2+J^2/r^2$. Rearranging yields $p_r^2=A-2du-Cu^2=Q(u)$.

Since $Q(0)=A>0$ and $Q((W-mc^2)/\kappa)=-J^2((W-mc^2)/\kappa)^2<0$, continuity gives a positive root below $(W-mc^2)/\kappa$. The other root is negative because the product of the roots is $-A/C<0$, so the positive root is unique. The quadratic formula gives the displayed $u_*$; $Q'(u_*)=-2(d+Cu_*)<0$, hence the root is simple. At this root $\mathcal E=W-\kappa u_*>mc^2$, so the momentum is real and the point lies in $D$.

Choose $x=r_*e_1$ and $p=(J/r_*)e_2$ at the turning point. The root equation in 2.1 gives $H(x,p)=W$, and [F2] gives a local solution. At the turn, direct differentiation gives $\dot p_r=c^2J^2/(\mathcal E r^3)+\kappa/r^2>0$, so $p_r$ changes from negative to positive. Since $p_r^2=Q(1/r)$ and 2.1 gives the unique positive root, $p_r$ cannot vanish again; consequently $r$ decreases on the incoming tail and increases on the outgoing tail. On every allowed state $0<u\le u_*<(W-mc^2)/\kappa$, hence $r\ge r_*$ and $mc^2<\mathcal E=W-\kappa u<W$, which gives $|p|<\sqrt A$. The force and velocity are bounded; on every finite time interval $x$ remains bounded and $|x|\ge r_*$, so the state stays in a compact subset of $D$ and [F2] extends it past every finite endpoint. Each monotone radial tail must be unbounded: if it had a finite limit greater than $r_*$, then $Q(1/r)$ and $\mathcal E$ would give $|\dot r|$ a positive lower bound, contradicting that finite limit. Thus $r\to\infty$ on both tails and $\dot r=c^2p_r/\mathcal E\to\pm c^2\sqrt A/W$, so $r$ grows linearly there. Then $|\dot p|=\kappa/r^2$ is integrable, and $p$ converges to incoming and outgoing limits of magnitude $\sqrt A$. Since the tangential momentum has magnitude $J/r\to0$, the limiting momenta point along the limiting radial directions, establishing the two asymptotes.

Orient the orbital plane so its polar angle increases with $J=|x\times p|$. Then $\dot\varphi=c^2J/(\mathcal E r^2)$ and $\dot r=c^2p_r/\mathcal E$, so $|d\varphi/du|=J/\sqrt{Q(u)}$ and the half-angle is $\Delta=\int_0^{u_*}J\,du/\sqrt{A-2du-Cu^2}$. Completing the square gives $Q=(d^2+CA)/C-C(u+d/C)^2$. With $y=(Cu+d)/\sqrt{d^2+CA}$, the root relation in 2.1 makes the endpoints $d/\sqrt{d^2+CA}$ and $1$, and the integral becomes $(J/\sqrt C)\int dy/\sqrt{1-y^2}=(J/\sqrt C)[\arcsin y]_{d/\sqrt{d^2+CA}}^1$. Put $\alpha=\arctan(\sqrt{CA}/d)\in(0,\pi/2)$. Since $\tan\alpha=\sqrt{CA}/d$, the Pythagorean identity and positivity of sine and cosine in [F3] give $\cos\alpha=d/\sqrt{d^2+CA}$; the quarter-turn identity then gives $\arcsin(d/\sqrt{d^2+CA})=\pi/2-\alpha$ because both angles lie in $[0,\pi/2]$. The evaluated integral is therefore $\Delta=(J/\sqrt C)\arctan(\sqrt{CA}/d)$.

Put $\alpha=\kappa/(cJ)\in(0,1)$, $q=\sqrt{1-\alpha^2}\in(0,1)$, and $\beta=\sqrt{1-m^2c^4/W^2}\in(0,1)$. If $a=\arcsin q$, then [F3] gives $a\in(0,\pi/2)$, $\sin a=q$, and $\cos a=\sqrt{1-q^2}>0$; hence $\tan a=q/\sqrt{1-q^2}$ and the principal inverse identity gives $a=\arctan(q/\sqrt{1-q^2})$. The formula from 3.2 becomes $\Delta=q^{-1}\arctan(\beta q/\sqrt{1-q^2})$; since $0<\beta<1$ and $\arctan$ is strictly increasing, $0<\Delta<\arcsin(q)/q$.

Define $g(x)=\sin x-2x/\pi$ on $[0,\pi/2]$. By [F3], $g(0)=g(\pi/2)=0$ and $g''(x)=-\sin x\le0$. Since $g'$ is differentiable and $g''\le0$, [F5] makes $g'$ nonincreasing. For any $0<x<\pi/2$, [F5] applied to $g$ on $[0,x]$ and $[x,\pi/2]$ gives $g(x)/x=g'(\xi_1)$ and $-g(x)/(\pi/2-x)=g'(\xi_2)$ for some $0<\xi_1<x<\xi_2<\pi/2$. Thus $g(x)/x\ge-g(x)/(\pi/2-x)$; multiplying by the positive $x(\pi/2-x)$ yields $g(x)\ge0$. Taking $x=\arcsin q$ gives $\arcsin q\le\pi q/2$, hence step 4.1 gives $\Delta<\pi/2$.

On either asymptotic tail, $|d\varphi/dr|=J/(r^2\sqrt{Q(1/r)})\sim J/(\sqrt A r^2)$. For every $0<\epsilon<1$, the definition of this limit bounds the integrand between $(1-\epsilon)J/(\sqrt A r^2)$ and $(1+\epsilon)J/(\sqrt A r^2)$ for all sufficiently large radii; integration from $r$ to infinity gives the angular gap $\delta(r)\sim J/(\sqrt A r)$. Step 3.1's asymptotic momentum and [F6] now give $r\sin\delta(r)\to J/\sqrt A$, the limiting perpendicular distance of each asymptotic line from the force center; this is $b$. The incoming momentum points opposite its limiting radial direction and the outgoing momentum along its own, so their angular separation is $\theta=\pi-2\Delta\in(0,\pi)$ by step 5.1.

The unique noncollision turning branch, impact parameter and exact deflection angle follow from steps 1.1–6.1. The hypotheses $W>mc^2$ and $J>\kappa/c$ are essential to the positive scattering root and are not relaxed.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

(a) [Components] For a field pair $(E,B)$ of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, define the
covariant components of the **electromagnetic two-form** $F$ in the chart by
$F_{00}=0$, $F_{0i}:=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}:=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$
($i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$) and $F_{ab}:=-F_{ba}$, the index-raised components being
$F^{0i}=E_i/c$, $F^{i0}=-E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. Here
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the spatial permutation symbol of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]. Then $F$ is a $C^k$ type-$(0,2)$
tensor field on $U$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], alternating at every event, and the
components above are exactly its component functions: at $p\in U$ the tensor
$F(p)$ is the bilinear form $F(p)(u,w)=F_{ab}(p)u^aw^b$ on $V$ in the
coordinates $u^a,w^b$ of $u,w$ in $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. Indeed each $F_{ab}$ is
a finite sum of products of the $C^k$ functions $E_i,B_k$ of the chart
coordinates with the constants $c,\epsilon_{ijk}$, hence a $C^k$ function of
$x(p)$, and the component criterion of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]] applies.
In the flat specialization, a named inertial chart with $x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres uses $F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, matching [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]].

Use the smooth, time-oriented Lorentzian background $(M,g,N)$, signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and the distinct chart, observer, congruence, tetrad and worldline meanings of [[def-rpm-spacetime-observer-and-worldline]]. The metric and time orientation are prescribed data, not dynamical variables. A **charged spinning test body** in this definition consists of the following model quantities along a massive worldline $z:I\to M$:

- $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval whose parameter is proper time $\tau$ in seconds; $z$ is $C^2$, future-directed and timelike, and $U:=dz/d\tau$ obeys $g(U,U)=-c^2$. The SI conversion constant is $c>0$ metres per second; in a flat specialization use the affine Minkowski model and the proper-time decomposition of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].
- The constant rest-mass parameter $m>0$ has unit kilogram, and the constant charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ has unit coulomb. They are primitive model parameters; this definition does not derive them from the background field or from another framework.
- The **kinetic four-momentum** is the derived vector $P:=mU$ along $z$, with unit kilogram metre per second. It is distinct from the potential-dependent covector defined in [[lem-rpm-charge-gauge-boundary]].
- The **spin or polarization vector** is a $C^1$ tangent vector field $s(\tau)\in T_{z(\tau)}M$ constrained by $g(s,U)=0$, so it lies in the positive-definite instantaneous rest space $U^\perp$. Its unit is angular momentum, kilogram metre squared per second. This is a classical model vector; no quantization or quantum spin state is defined here.
- The gyromagnetic ratio $g_s\in\mathbb R$ is a dimensionless primitive species parameter. In the instantaneous rest space the model defines the magnetic-moment vector by $\mu=(g_s q/2m)s$, with unit ampere metre squared. No value $g_s=2$ is assumed, and this constitutive relation is not deduced from Lorentz covariance or classical electromagnetism.
- The prescribed external electromagnetic field is a $C^1$ alternating covariant two-tensor $F$ on an open region of $M$, independent of the unknown curve. Define $F^\sharp:T M\to T M$ by $g(F^\sharp(v),w)=F(w,v)$. In the flat specialization, a named inertial chart with $x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres uses $F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, matching [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]]. On the curved background, $F$ is only a two-form; at an event its components in a chosen orthonormal tetrad use the same algebraic convention. Such a tetrad is a basis field, not a coordinate chart or an observer congruence, as distinguished in [[def-rpm-spacetime-observer-and-worldline]]. The components in an orthonormal tetrad have tesla units. This is an explicit curved-background model input. The cited EM supplier is a flat Minkowski definition and does not derive a curved field or curved Maxwell system.
- On any open potential domain where a $C^2$ covector field $A$ exists, $F=dA$ with components $F_{ab}=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a$ and $A$ has tesla metre components in the stated coordinates. No global potential is assumed, and no Maxwell equation or constitutive law is imposed here.

This is a test-body model on a fixed background: self-gravity, gravitational backreaction, self-field evaluation, radiation reaction, collisions, electric dipole moments, field-gradient translational forces and higher multipoles are outside this definition. Units follow the framework-local SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and do not identify quantities across frameworks.

Assume the charged test-body quantities and local potential domain of [[def-rpm-charge-spin-model]], the flat-space sign convention of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], and the adopted fixed-endpoint action postulate [[post-rpm-external-charge-action]], and assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure. For a finite $C^2$ future-timelike curve segment $z:[a,b]\to O$ in that domain, where $a<b$ are proper-time endpoints, and the local $C^2$ fixed-endpoint variations of the postulate, choose the orientation-preserving parameter $\lambda=\tau$; the segment is stationary for the adopted action if and only if

$$m\nabla_UU=qF^\sharp(U),\qquad (\nabla_UU)_a=\frac qm F_{ab}U^b.$$

This is a model deduction: it establishes the equation equivalent to stationarity of the postulated functional, not the physical truth of the postulate.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$; assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for its canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure, so the metric-selected Levi–Civita connection $\nabla$ exists by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]. Let $O\subseteq M$ be open and let $F$ be a $C^1$ alternating covariant two-tensor field on $O$ (a two-form); define $F^\sharp$ by $g(F^\sharp(v),w)=F(w,v)$. Fix $m,c>0$, $q\in\mathbb R$, an event $x_0\in O$, and $U_0\in T_{x_0}M$ with $g(U_0,U_0)=-c^2$ future directed. Then the initial-value problem

$$\dot x=U,\qquad \nabla_UU=(q/m)F^\sharp(U),\qquad (x(\tau_0),U(\tau_0))=(x_0,U_0)$$

has a unique local $C^2$ solution on an open proper-time interval containing $\tau_0$. Any two solutions with these initial data agree on every connected part of their common domain containing $\tau_0$. Along the solution, $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ remains future directed. The result is local; it asserts no completeness or global existence for arbitrary external fields.

Adopt [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]] and
[[post-sr-ideal-massless-particle-momentum]]. Then the following conditional
physical claims hold in the flat classical model, with the units of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]].

**(a) Massive particle.** Let a massive particle have constant mass $m>0$,
four-momentum $P=mU$ and a future unit observer $n$. Its measured energy
$E_n(P)=-c\,\eta(P,n)$, spatial momentum $q_n(P)=h(P)$ and kinetic energy
$T_n(P)=E_n(P)-mc^2$ satisfy $E_n(P)>0$, $T_n(P)\ge0$ and the mass-shell
identity $E_n(P)^2=m^2c^4+c^2|q_n(P)|^2$; $T_n(P)=0$ if and only if the
particle is at rest in the observer's frame ($U=cn$). In an inertial frame
whose stationary observer is $n=e_0$, the components are $P=(E/c,\mathbf p)$
with $E=E_{e_0}(P)=m\gamma_wc^2$ and $\mathbf p=m\gamma_w\mathbf w\in\mathbb R^3$
the coordinates of $q_{e_0}(P)=\sum_{i=1}^3p^ie_i$
for the coordinate velocity $\mathbf w$, and under a passive boost the
components transform as the components of the vector $P$; the combination
$E^2-c^2|\mathbf p|^2=m^2c^4$ is frame-independent.

**(b) Four-force.** Along a $C^2$ worldline with four-acceleration $A$, the
four-force $F=\dot P$ satisfies $\eta(P,F)=0$ and $F=mA$; in an inertial frame
$F=\gamma\,(\mathbf f\cdot\mathbf w/c,\ \mathbf f)$ and
$dE/dt=\mathbf f\cdot\mathbf w$, where $\mathbf f=d\mathbf p/dt$ is the
coordinate three-force. The constancy of $m$ is used; if instead $m$ is a
$C^1$ function $m:I\to(0,\infty)$ along the same worldline, define $P:=mU$
and $F:=\dot P$ by the general derivative construction. As a mathematical identity, $\eta(P,F)=-mc^2\,dm/d\tau$, and the
constant-mass identities are not transferred to variable-mass systems.

**(c) System mass.** For a finite nonempty system of particles all of whose
four-momenta are nonzero future causal, let $Q:=\sum_iP_i$. If $Q$ is
future timelike, its invariant mass $M=\sqrt{-\eta(Q,Q)}/c$ satisfies: in the
center-of-momentum frame with $e_0=Q/(Mc)$ one has
$Mc^2=\sum_iE_{e_0}(P_i)$; every massive constituent has
$E_{e_0}(P_i)\ge m_ic^2$, with equality exactly when it is at rest in that
frame, and every massless constituent has $E_{e_0}(P_i)>0$. Hence
$M\ge\sum_im_i$ over the massive constituents, with equality if and only if
the system is massive-only and all its constituents are at rest in the
center-of-momentum frame. If $Q$ is future null, then $M=0$, all constituents
are massless with parallel momenta, and no center-of-momentum frame exists.

**(d) Massless particle.** An ideal massless particle has
$E_n(P)=c\,|q_n(P)|>0$, has no rest frame and is not $mU$ for any $m>0$; it is
not obtained from the massive formula by setting $m=0$.

**(e) Necessary collision thresholds.** Suppose that, under the adopted
isolated-collision balance, an isolated collision occurs whose incoming legs
are massive particles of constant masses $m_1,\dots,m_N$ and whose outgoing
legs are massive particles of masses $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_K$ and possibly ideal
massless particles. Let $M$ be the invariant mass of the common total
four-momentum $Q$. Then the necessary inequalities $M\ge\sum_im_i$ and
$M\ge\sum_j\mu_j$ hold; if the incoming side is a projectile of mass $m_1$
and a target of mass $m_2$ at rest in the observer frame of the target, with
projectile energy $E$ and kinetic energy $T=E-m_1c^2$ in that frame, then

$$E\ \ge\ \frac{c^2}{2m_2}\Bigl[\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^K\mu_j\Bigr)^2-m_1^2-m_2^2\Bigr],\qquad T\ \ge\ \frac{c^2}{2m_2}\Bigl[\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^K\mu_j\Bigr)^2-(m_1+m_2)^2\Bigr],$$

Separately, under the same adopted balance, a single incoming massless particle
cannot produce an outgoing state containing a massive particle. These are kinematic necessity statements under
the adopted conservation: they do not assert that any collision occurs, do
not fix probabilities, amplitudes or cross sections, and are not empirical
findings.

**(f) Scope.** All clauses are conditional on the two postulates and on the
stated idealisations; the conclusions carry the same idealisations. No
measurement, precision, statistical or empirical claim is made.

Let the laboratory region, its inertial chart and the fields and sources be those
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], with the
units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; fix the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the chart and the oriented volume form $\varepsilon$ of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]], with $\varepsilon_{0123}=+1$ and
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$.

(a) [Components] For a field pair $(E,B)$ of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, define the
covariant components of the **electromagnetic two-form** $F$ in the chart by
$F_{00}=0$, $F_{0i}:=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}:=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$
($i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$) and $F_{ab}:=-F_{ba}$, the index-raised components being
$F^{0i}=E_i/c$, $F^{i0}=-E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. Here
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the spatial permutation symbol of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]. Then $F$ is a $C^k$ type-$(0,2)$
tensor field on $U$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], alternating at every event, and the
components above are exactly its component functions: at $p\in U$ the tensor
$F(p)$ is the bilinear form $F(p)(u,w)=F_{ab}(p)u^aw^b$ on $V$ in the
coordinates $u^a,w^b$ of $u,w$ in $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. Indeed each $F_{ab}$ is
a finite sum of products of the $C^k$ functions $E_i,B_k$ of the chart
coordinates with the constants $c,\epsilon_{ijk}$, hence a $C^k$ function of
$x(p)$, and the component criterion of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]] applies.

(b) [Observer decomposition] Let $n:=e_0$ be the future unit timelike vector of
the chart and let $e_a:=F_{ab}n^b$, $b_a:=(*F)_{ab}n^b$ be the observer
components of [[thm-sr-antisymmetric-observer-decomposition]]; then
$e_i=+E_i/c$, $b_i=-B_i$ and $e_0=b_0=0$, and the invariants and square wedge
of that theorem read

$$\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2,\qquad F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=+4\,(E\cdot B)/c,\qquad F\wedge F=-2\,(E\cdot B)\,\varepsilon/c,$$

where $|\cdot|$ and $\cdot$ are the spatial Euclidean structure of the frame.
(For the same pair $(E,B)$, that theorem's optional clause (d) uses
$F_{\rm optional}^{i0}=E_i/c$ and $F_{\rm optional}^{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, so
$F_{\rm optional}=-F$ in all six components, not only the magnetic block. This
framework fixes clause (a) and uses the theorem's general algebra; its optional
SI dictionary must be converted by negating the entire tensor.)

$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$, and
$A^\mu:=(\varphi/c,A)$, $A_\mu:=\eta_{\mu\nu}A^\nu$, then
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$; conversely, if a $C^1$

-\partial_\nu A_\mu$, then $E,B$ recovered from $F$ by clause (a) obey
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ with
$\varphi:=-cA_0$ and the spatial potential vector $A:=(A_1,A_2,A_3)$. Here
$\nabla$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] in the spatial coordinates,
and the spatial cross-product conventions of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] are
used. The definition does not assert that every field pair admits such a
potential; where a $C^1$ potential represents the $C^1$-or-better field of
clause (a), the field is closed in the explicit sense
$\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}=0$. This conclusion does not require second
classical derivatives of the potential: put
$H_{\lambda\mu\nu}:=\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}$, which is continuous because $F$ is $C^1$; for
every smooth compactly supported test $\psi$, substituting $F=dA$ and
integrating by parts twice, moving the derivatives first onto $\psi$
([[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]] (b)) and then off the
potential factors after commuting only the smooth test derivatives
([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]), gives $\int H\psi=0$; the
fundamental lemma (a) of [[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]]
then gives $H=0$. The framework's potential theorems establish existence only
under their stated hypotheses; [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]
supplies the coordinate derivatives $\partial_\mu$ used throughout.

(d) [Four-current and index-raising operator] With the adopted four-current
$j=(c\rho,J)$ of [[def-em-sources]], the raised-index operator $\Phi$ of
[[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]], defined pointwise on $V$ by

$\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$; the components of $F$
carry the tesla (T), those of $j$ carry A m$^{-2}$, and those of a
four-potential $A^\mu$ carry T m.

With the covector convention $A_0=-\phi/c$ and $A_i=\mathbf A_i$, they give $F_{01}=-E_0/c$, $F_{ij}=0$, hence exactly the field in [F1]. Thus the action potential-domain hypothesis [A1] is met, and under the exact assumption [A3], [F2] gives its covariant Lorentz-force equation.

Apply [F3] under [A3] to this field: $\dot p_1=F_0$, $\dot{\mathbf p}_\perp=0$, and $\dot{\mathcal E}=F_0v_1$. Integration with the initial data gives $p_1(t)=p_{01}+F_0t$ and constant $\mathbf p_\perp$. By adopted [A2] and the inertial momentum relations [F4], $\mathcal E^2=m^2c^4+c^2|\mathbf p|^2$; since $\mathcal E=\gamma mc^2>0$, this is $\mathcal E=c\sqrt{m^2c^2+|\mathbf p|^2}$, while $\mathbf p=\gamma m\mathbf v$ gives $\mathbf v=c^2\mathbf p/\mathcal E$. Thus the definitions of $\Pi,\mathcal E,\mathbf v$ in the statement follow. Differentiating the shell identity with $\dot{\mathbf p}=F_0e_1$ gives $2\mathcal E\dot{\mathcal E}=2c^2p_1F_0$, hence $\dot{\mathcal E}=c^2p_1F_0/\mathcal E=F_0v_1$, as required by [F3]. Since $m,c>0$, the square-root denominator is at least $mc>0$, and [F5] gives subluminal motion.

Suppose $F_0\ne0$. Differentiating the proposed $x^1(t)$ and using $\dot p_1=F_0$ gives $\dot x^1=cp_1/\sqrt{\Pi^2+p_1^2}=v_1$. For the transverse formula, the derivative of $\log(p+\sqrt{\Pi^2+p^2})$ is $1/\sqrt{\Pi^2+p^2}$: the argument is positive since $\sqrt{\Pi^2+p^2}>|p|$, and the identity follows from [F6, F7] and the chain rule. Hence $\dot{\mathbf x}_\perp=c\mathbf p_\perp/\sqrt{\Pi^2+p_1^2}=\mathbf v_\perp$. At $t=0$ both position increments vanish, so these formulas have the prescribed initial position and velocity.

If $F_0=0$, [F3] makes $\mathbf p$ and $\mathcal E$ constant, so the displayed free position has derivative $c^2\mathbf p_0/\mathcal E(0)=\mathbf v$ and the initial position. Its speed is below $c$ by [F5].

In either case the constructed curve satisfies the force equation and the initial data by steps 2.1–2.2. Any other solution has the same momentum by integrating [F3]; subtracting its position from the displayed one gives a differentiable vector with zero derivative and zero initial value, so each component vanishes by [F8]. Thus it agrees throughout any common connected interval. The formulas have positive square-root arguments and positive logarithm arguments for every finite $t$, so they extend smoothly over all $\mathbb R$.

These are exactly the velocity components from step 2.1, and all increments vanish at $t=0$. For $\Omega=0$, the stated free position has constant derivative $c\mathbf p_0/S_0=\mathbf v$.

The transverse coordinates relative to the fixed centre $(x^1_0+B,x^2_0-A)$ are $(A\sin\Omega t-B\cos\Omega t,\,B\sin\Omega t+A\cos\Omega t)$; their squared distance from that centre is $A^2+B^2$. Since $S_0=\gamma_0mc$ and $|\Omega|=|qB_0|/(\gamma_0m)$, the radius is $c|\mathbf p_\perp|/(S_0|\Omega|)=|\mathbf p_\perp|/|qB_0|$. If $\mathbf p_\perp=0$, both transverse velocity components vanish; if $p_{03}=0$, $x^3$ is constant. The energy constancy in step 2.1 proves zero magnetic work.

The displayed curves satisfy the force equation and initial data by steps 2.1 and 3.1. Any other solution with the same data has constant energy $\mathcal E=cS_0$ by [F3], so step 2.1 puts its momentum in the same constant-coefficient system $\dot p_1=\Omega p_2$, $\dot p_2=-\Omega p_1$, $\dot p_3=0$. For the difference $d$ of two such momenta, the product rule [F9] gives $\frac d{dt}(d_1^2+d_2^2)=2\Omega d_1d_2-2\Omega d_2d_1=0$, and $\dot d_3=0$. With zero initial difference, [F7] makes $d_1^2+d_2^2=d_3=0$ on every common connected interval, hence both momenta agree, including $\Omega=0$. Their velocities then agree by [F4], so each position difference has zero derivative and zero initial value; [F7] gives equality. The formulas are smooth for all real $t$; $S_0\ge mc>0$, and in the rotating case the denominator $\Omega$ is nonzero. The resulting worldline is timelike by [F5].
